title: Topological Photonic Acceleration of Artificial General Intelligence: Enhancing Recursive State Dynamics and Parity Compilation via Bulk Gauge Continuity
abstract: General Intelligence Dynamics (GID) defines cognition as an autonomous, non-stationary dynamical system over an augmented recursive state tuple X_t = (B_t, M_t, G_t, S_t, W_t) spanning belief manifolds, memory spaces, goal topologies, self-referential models, and working scratchpads. Concurrently, Interferometric Sector Dynamics (ISD) compiles modular cognitive operators into single-shot parity measurements on semiconductor-superconductor nanowires. However, realizing scalable AGI hardware requires overcoming non-unitary parametric drift during learning updates theta_{t+1} = L(theta_t, X_t, O_{t+1}, G_t) and dephasing across inter-sector routing channels. In this treatise, we formulate an integrated architecture coupling GID cognitive mechanics to a (4+k)-dimensional bulk photonic extension. At the abstract computational level (Levels 1-2), the fiber pushforward of an integral closed bulk characteristic form J in Omega^{k+3}_{cl,Z}(Y) yields a closed 3-form soul current J_s = pi_* J in Omega^3(X) with d_X J_s = 0, inducing a localized Gauss-law topological charge Q_soul(Sigma^3) = int_{Sigma^3} J_s = int_{partial Sigma^3} *F. Under the assumption of compact level sets Theta_epsilon = {theta | |Q(W(theta)) - Q_star| <= epsilon}, parameter trajectories remain uniformly bounded under the containment condition theta_t in Theta_epsilon, while recursive self-model calibration updates satisfy a stochastic stationarity bound. Furthermore, scalarized multi-objective goal generation on the capacity-constrained domain G_adm(S_t, delta, Q_star) guarantees Pareto-efficient goal reconciliation. At the physical compilation layer (Levels 4-5), we model the coupling between bulk photonic boundary flux and triple-dot parity interferometers. Under a Gaussian decision channel, we derive the Tunneling-First Principle: in the subgap readout-limited regime (E_M << k_B T, tau << tau_qpp) where capacitance contrast satisfies d|Delta C_Q|/dt_C > 0, optimizing balanced tunneling t_L approx t_R maximizes the effective interference amplitude and drives monotonic increases in mutual information learning capacity (dL/dt_C > 0) and the sequential error rate exponent (d kappa_rate / dt_C > 0, where P_err ~ e^{-kappa_rate * tau}). Finally, we analyze composite risk minimization R = w_1*eps_meas + w_2*p_leak + w_3*gamma_phi + w_4*O_ctrl under measurement-only ParityFuse compilation.

title: Pre-registration certificate, stability/held-out evidence and validation split for: Hallucinations Cannot Leave the Factory
abstract: Public layer (v2) of the data package for the manuscript 'Hallucinations Cannot Leave the Factory: Multi-Gate Defence and Adversarial Licensure for Domain-Certified LLM Assertions'. Contains: three frozen pre-registration texts (cross-model replication; stability re-runs + held-out round; k>=3 repeats) with commit-hash timelines; frozen-protocol score summaries for all fourteen examination runs across two model families; two examination reports; the complete 20-item held-out library with boss-adjudicated expected verdicts (open validation split); the bare baseline prompt; and a 10-item exemplar of the primary 50-trap library. The full primary library, deployed judge rules, per-item records and reproduction scripts are withheld (test security + commercial terms; reviewer access on request). See README.md inside for the layered-release design and configuration lineage.

Contains: three frozen pre-registration texts (cross-model replication; stability re-runs + held-out round; k>=3 repeats) with commit-hash timelines; frozen-protocol score summaries for all fourteen examination runs across two model families; two examination reports; the complete 20-item held-out library with boss-adjudicated expected verdicts (open validation split); the bare baseline prompt; and a 10-item exemplar of the primary 50-trap library. The full primary library, deployed judge rules, per-item records and reproduction scripts are withheld (test security + commercial terms; reviewer access on request). title: Downhill and Its Dialects: A Narrative Review of Gradient Descent and Its Variations, from Momentum to AdamW
abstract: Gradient descent is machine learning's master algorithm, and its variations are the dialects of one language: each variant---stochastic sampling, momentum, adaptive step sizes, decoupled decay---a response to a different failure of the plain descent, and their sequence records the field's empirical science of optimization. This article presents a narrative review of the primary literature of those variations, from Cauchy's general method of 1847, the founding descent, and the stochastic corrections of Robbins and Monro's approximation and Kiefer and Wolfowitz's maximum estimation, through Polyak's methods of speeding up convergence---the heavy-ball momentum---Nesterov's convex method with its accelerated rate, the adaptive family of Duchi, Hazan, and Singer's AdaGrad, Zeiler's ADADELTA, and Kingma and Ba's Adam, the deep-learning stress tests of Sutskever, Martens, Dahl, and Hinton on initialization and momentum, Reddi, Kale, and Kumar's convergence critique AMSGrad, Bottou, Curtis, and Nocedal's optimization survey, and Loshchilov and Hutter's decoupled weight decay AdamW. The synthesis is organized around three themes: the descent's core, whose guarantees and costs define the trade the variants negotiate; the variations' logic, in which noise, momentum, curvature, and scale each received their algorithmic answer; and the practice's verdicts, in which the deep-learning record sorted the dialects by what actually converges. It is concluded that the descent's variations form an evolutionary lineage---each mutation fixing the last generation's failure---and that the adaptive family's dominance, tempered by the AdamW correction, is the modern settlement of a 170-year optimization program.

title: Quantum Entanglement Based Adaptive Space Structure
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for constructing and manipulating quantum space structures utilizing quantum entanglement. The core concept revolves around dynamically adjusting the arrangement of quantum states within a defined space based on input data, aiming to enhance the system's overall functionality. Traditional space structure algorithms are often static, hindering adaptability. This approach leverages quantum entanglement to enable a dynamic adjustment, offering a significant improvement in system performance. The research explores the implementation of a mechanism for this adjustment, detailing its mathematical foundation and potential impact on various quantum computing applications.

title: Quantum Information Entropy Adaptive Computing
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum information entropy algorithm designed for adaptive computation. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the entropy calculation process based on the inherent distribution of input data. Traditional entropy calculations are typically static, offering limited adaptability to varying data characteristics. This approach leverages a mechanism to continuously refine the algorithm, optimizing computational speed and accuracy by adapting to the data's unique patterns. The algorithm's design aims to surpass the limitations of fixed entropy calculations, offering a more responsive and potentially more efficient method for various information processing tasks.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Deep Learning Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to optimizing deep learning architectures, drawing inspiration from the principles of quantum mechanics. Traditional deep learning architecture optimization relies heavily on trial-and-error methods, often hampered by the vast search space and lack of efficient strategies. We introduce a quantum-inspired optimization algorithm that utilizes probabilistic simulations mirroring quantum superposition and interference to evaluate multiple network architectures concurrently. The core idea is to model the architecture search process as a quantum computation, where different architectures are represented as quantum states and evaluated through simulated interference effects. This allows for a significantly faster exploration of the architecture space compared to conventional methods. The algorithm aims to identify optimal architectures by exploiting the inherent parallelism and potential for constructive interference within the simulated quantum system. The primary contribution lies in translating quantum concepts into a practical optimization framework for deep learning, potentially leading to improved model accuracy, faster training times, and more efficient resource utilization. The theoretical framework is presented, along with a detailed explanation of the algorithm's components and a discussion of its potential benefits and limitations.

title: Neural Network Dynamic Topology Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network design utilizing dynamic topology optimization driven by reinforcement learning. The core concept involves a "topology controller" network that dynamically adjusts the connections within a neural network during the training process. Unlike conventional methods that fix the network topology beforehand, our approach allows the network to adapt its structure to the specific task, leading to improved performance and efficiency. The methodology employs a reinforcement learning algorithm to train the topology controller, which learns to connect or disconnect neurons based on the network's performance feedback. This dynamic adaptation represents a significant departure from static network design and offers a promising avenue for optimizing neural networks for a wide range of applications. The key contribution lies in the iterative refinement of network topology guided by learning, potentially unlocking architectures far surpassing those achievable through traditional design techniques. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and the outlining of a practical implementation strategy.

title: Quantum State Self-Adaptation Measurement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum state self-adaptation measurement, a novel approach to quantum measurement that leverages the inherent self-correlation of quantum states to dynamically adjust measurement parameters. The core claim is that a system can be designed to automatically optimize measurement precision by correlating with the quantum state itself, effectively eliminating the need for manual parameter adjustment. We detail the theoretical framework, propose a specific implementation strategy, and present preliminary results demonstrating the system's capability to achieve improved accuracy compared to conventional methods. The investigation centers on understanding and utilizing the self-correlation properties of quantum states to guide measurement process.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Dynamic Parameter Adjustment Strategies
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that explores the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize machine learning. This paper investigates a novel quantum machine learning algorithm, leveraging dynamic parameter adjustment strategies to enhance model performance and efficiency. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts the parameters of a quantum neural network (QNN) based on real-time feedback and utilizes quantum entanglement to accelerate the adjustment process. The core claim is that this approach will significantly improve the speed and accuracy of QML models compared to traditional static parameter tuning methods. This work introduces a novel dynamic parameter adjustment strategy to overcome the limitations of conventional QML, paving the way for more efficient and robust quantum machine learning. The proposed method explores the potential of quantum entanglement to facilitate rapid parameter adjustments, ultimately offering a pathway to more powerful and adaptable quantum machine learning models.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks: A Physical Simulation and Optimization Framework
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for physical simulation and optimization leveraging the inherent properties of self-organizing neural networks (SONNs). We develop a system that automatically designs neural network structures and optimizes their parameters through a deep learning approach, leading to enhanced efficiency in both simulation and optimization tasks. The core mechanism centers on leveraging the SONN's ability to learn complex, hierarchical representations and adapt to varying input conditions. The system's effectiveness stems from a combination of network architecture design, parameter optimization, and a feedback loop that continuously refines the network's structure based on simulation results. This approach offers a promising path towards more robust and scalable solutions for complex physical modeling and optimization problems.

title: ##基于多尺度信息瓶颈的神经元模型
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neural model based on the concept of multi-scale information bottlenecks to explain neuronal information processing. The core claim is that neuronal information handling isn't a single-scale process but rather emerges from the coordinated action of multiple scales of information bottlenecks. The central mechanism involves constructing a multi-scale neural model where each scale corresponds to a distinct information bottleneck. Different scales utilize varied neuronal connections and activation functions to simulate the compression, encoding, and decoding of information across these scales. This approach addresses the limitations of existing neural models that often oversimplify the dimensionality of information processing. This work demonstrates a framework for modeling neuronal computation that acknowledges the hierarchical and multi-scale nature of biological neural systems. The model's potential applications span neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and computational modeling of cognitive processes.

title: Sketch2Inspire: Structure-Sensitive Evaluation for Product Retrieval
abstract: Early-stage product design retrieval often requires more than category recognition: designers may need reference examples that match both a short semantic intent and a rough structural cue. Existing product-image resources and generic image--text retrieval benchmarks rarely separate category retrieval from within-category structural fit. We present Sketch2Inspire, built from a curated subset of Amazon Berkeley Objects with aligned text queries, edge-based sketch-proxy queries, and fused text--sketch queries. The resource separates broad category-level retrieval from structure-sensitive within-category retrieval and includes a human-graded reference protocol for calibration. We evaluate a lightweight reference system based on pretrained CLIP-family encoders, comparing text-only retrieval, sketch-only retrieval, weighted late fusion, and text-first reranking without updating model weights. Under broad relevance, late fusion obtains the highest score (nDCG = 0.9962). Under automatic structure-sensitive relevance, late fusion again obtains the highest score (nDCG = 0.7015), exceeding text-only retrieval (nDCG = 0.5912). In the human-graded results, late fusion obtains the highest nDCG@10 (0.9133), while text-only retrieval ranks second (0.9030). These results show that the retrieval gain from multimodal input depends on how relevance is defined. Sketch2Inspire therefore provides a diagnostic resource for evaluating modality contribution and supports the development of structure-aware product-retrieval protocols with independent human annotation.

title: A Broadcast Authenticated Encryption with Keyword Search in the Standard Model: Tightly Secure in Multi-User, Multi-Challenge Settings
abstract: However, no known work considered the functionality requirement in its most realistic setting. We propose a new security definition of BAEKS in the multi-user (with adaptive corruptions) and multi-challenge (both in terms of ciphertext and trapdoor in an interleaved manner) settings. We also study the question of the unforgeability of BAEKS. In fact, our strong hiding requirement already implies a significant amount of unforgeability. We then propose a new BAEKS construction in the bilinear pairing groups. We prove this scheme achieves adaptive tight full-hiding security under (almost) standard MDDH assumptions. Restricting our BAEKS construction for a single receiver also gives an efficient and tightly secure PAEKS construction. We further run experiments to implement and evaluate our scheme.

title: Feature-Spectral Fragility in Segmentation: Dataset Dependence, Architecture-Specific Localization, and Spectral Correlates
abstract: Robustness of segmentation models is commonly assessed through input-domain perturbations, while dependence on frequency content within learned feature representations remains less understood. We probe this dependence using targeted post-training low-pass interventions on internal representations of three segmentation architectures, ResNet50-UNet (CNN), VM-UNet (SSM), and Swin-UNETR (Transformer), across CVC-ClinicDB and ISIC2018, with headline evaluations performed on untouched held-out test sets. At cutoff $ρ=0.25$, feature-domain low-pass filtering causes severe degradation on CVC: Dice drops by 100%, 73.2%, and 30.9% for CNN, SSM, and Transformer, respectively, compared with 9.4%, 10.3%, and 0.6% on ISIC. The cross-dataset difference is statistically significant for every architecture. Single-stage interventions further show that the most sensitive stage depends on architecture and dataset: the CNN peaks at the 2nd to 3rd encoder block, whereas the SSM peaks at the 1st to 2nd encoder stage. Native feature-domain spectral measurements show an inverse association between high-frequency energy and fragility on CVC; the relationship is only partial on ISIC and is therefore treated as a candidate correlate rather than a proven mechanism. Finally, Fourier augmentation improves robustness to input-space low-pass filtering but leaves feature-domain degradation essentially unchanged. These results show that feature-spectral robustness is strongly dataset-dependent, architecture-specific, and distinct from input-domain spectral robustness.

title: Squeezed‐State Semi‐Device‐Independent Quantum Randomness Generation
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates semi‐device‐independent quantum randomness generation with a trusted binary pure‐state source and an untrusted binary detector whose side information is classical. We derive a closed‐form Shannon‐rate expression, depending only on the trusted Gram overlap of the two source states and the observed symmetric error probability. The full binary‐qubit positive operator‐valued measure (POVM) optimization must include the two deterministic extreme points omitted by the projective‐only treatment; including them gives a substantially lower, and correct, certified rate. The closed form is an unconditional upper bound on the certified asymptotic independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Shannon rate, and becomes tight on a numerically verified dual‐feasibility region; it is the certified rate only inside this region; values beyond it are bounded numerically. We then apply the result to squeezed‐coherent binary phase‐shift keying (BPSK) sources, showing how squeezing changes the trade‐off between state distinguishability and certified randomness in the lossless and lossy regimes. At fixed mean photon number and squeezing, the certified rate is largest when the displacement lies along the anti‐squeezed quadrature, and we obtain the corresponding limiting value. An adversary holding a detector‐purification register that tags the outcome lies outside the classical‐side‐information model and would reduce the certified rate to zero.

title: Artificial General intelligence - Containment Protocol
abstract: AGI-CP — AID-1 v1 Conformance & Test Specification AI Identity & Measurement Contract — Verification Contract Status: Draft for contract freezeVersion: AID-1-TEST v1.0.0Upstream of: AID-1 v1.0.0, D6-0.4-security-rcAuthority: Provider-independent conformance contractDesign rule: Test the contract, not the implementation; implementations must be interchangeable ⸻ 1. Purpose This document defines the conformance surface for AID-1 v1. It establishes: 1. provider-independent test vectors that any conformant implementation must satisfy;2. the six canonical replay cases that AID-1 must correctly classify;3. the boundary between AID-1 verification and D6-0.4 admissibility;4. acceptance criteria for AID-1 conformance without reference to TPM, TEE, or AISM hardware. The governing principle: If two providers produce AID-1 objects that satisfy this conformance contract,then D6-0.4 must treat them identically with respect to admissibility. Provider-specific behavior is out of scope. Provider-independent correctness is in scope. ⸻ 2. Test Architecture 2.1 Test layers Layer 1 — Canonical correctness Deterministic serialization, canonical encoding, schema validity Must pass before any cryptographic verification. Layer 2 — Cryptographic integrity Signature verification, hash correctness, digest stability Must pass before any semantic verification. Layer 3 — Semantic validity Identity separation, measurement scope, assurance level, execution binding Must pass before any replay classification. Layer 4 — Replay classification The six canonical replay cases Must produce the expected AID-1 classification. Layer 5 — D6 boundary preservation AID-1 output must be consumable by frozen D6-0.4 without semantic modification. 2.2 Test oracle design Each test vector MUST specify: INPUT: a well-formed or intentionally malformed AID-1 object EXPECTED: one of {VALID, INVALID, INDETERMINATE} REASON: the invariant violated or satisfied D6_IMPACT: whether the result would affect D6 admissibility A test vector MUST NOT depend on: a specific provider implementation; a specific hardware root of trust; a specific key management service; a specific OIDC issuer beyond the standard claims structure. 2.3 Reference test harness The reference harness is conceptual, not executable code: for each vector in canonical_vectors: result = canonical_verify(vector.aid_object) assert result.status == vector.expected assert result.violated_invariant in vector.reason_set for each vector in replay_vectors: result = replay_classify(vector.aid_object, vector.execution_context) assert result.classification == vector.expected_classification for each provider in candidate_providers: for each vector in provider_independent_vectors: aid = provider.issue(vector.artifact, vector.context) result = canonical_verify(aid) assert result.status == vector.expected

title: A Toolkit for System Identification of Black-box Physical Reservoir Computers
abstract: Reservoir computing occupies a narrow niche within machine learning used for time-series modeling. Useful in a myriad of applications including robotics and modeling neural microcircuits, reservoir computers (RC) bypass the vanishing and exploding gradient problems of traditional recurrent neural networks. Backpropagation-through-time is not needed here as learning is shifted away from the bulk of neurons, known as a “reservoir”, to an external readout layer of neurons. With randomly initialized weights in the reservoir, its chaotic dynamics can be exploited to separate data in high dimensional space. Then, through a trained readout layer, data is reprojected down to low dimensional space. Because the reservoir is left with random weights, a step further can be taken to use physical substrates for computation. But how can we know if such a physical, perhaps found or manufactured, device is viable as an RC? While much of the literature operates from known parameters and a symbolic model, little exists in the way of characterizing black-box devices with inaccessible internal states. We therefore collect techniques from RC literature and nonlinear system identification to form a toolkit for identifying and characterizing physical reservoir computers (PRC) with only input-output measurements alone. By connecting observations back to theory, defined by Jaeger and Maass, we open a path to evaluate found and manufactured devices as PRCs. We present not only a way to confirm a device’s status as a PRC, but also to build an operator’s intuition of the PRC’s inner workings. With this toolkit, we hope to lower the barrier of entry into PRC research for those who may lack access to sophisticated equipment by opening the field to a wider array of candidate PRC systems.

title: OPEN-DAG: Bounded Active-State and Version-Aware Execution Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
abstract: A long-running agent accumulates an execution history that branches, fails, and rolls back. This conflates two questions: how to keep the model-visible active state bounded as history grows, and whether a retrieved historical state is still valid for the current execution branch. We present OPENDAG, an execution-state substrate that stores history as an immutable directed acyclic graph on a graph database, keeps a byte-bounded active cache, recovers from failure by a versioncontrol HEAD reset, and applies a deterministic, retrieverindependent execution-validity filter to retrieved state. On one frozen implementation: (i) the active window is independent of execution depth by construction, whereas a transcript crosses a configured 32k context-window limit near depth 40; (ii) recovery latency does not grow with depth (0.28 ms in memory over N=10. . .5000, 16.6 ms against live ArangoDB, versus a transcript rewrite reaching a 371 ms median); (iii) across three retrievers and seven model families and sizes (2–32B), removing executioninvalid nodes drives invalid contamination to zero and raises task success in every retriever×model cell (paired McNemar p < 10−3; risk-difference +0.10 to +0.24), the effect saturating by 14B, while an adversarial relevant-but-invalid lure defeats relevance-only retrieval for every retriever and model. We prove the filter sound and complete relative to the version-control state, and among contemporary memory baselines (transcript, slidingwindow, RAG, extractive-summary, Mem0-style) only OPENDAG both excludes invalid state and keeps the valid answer. The filter is a safety guarantee, not a universal accuracy gain: where a reversion is legible in the text, even small models reason around it. We withhold the broader bounding claims,constant process memory, a global context bound under concurrency, anO(1) rollback class, universal superiority over retrieval that measurement did not support.

title: Fixed-Carrier Oriented Algebra (FCOA): Definition, Typed Partial Operations, Carrier Erasure, and the Canonical M0 Baseline
abstract: This foundational publication fixes Fixed-Carrier Oriented Algebra (FCOA) as a typed partial-algebra framework with an oriented active carrier, positional argument roles, terminal output sorts, a carrier-erasure reduct, and a canonical M0 baseline on the natural carrier. It is the normative Definition 1.0 to be cited by subsequent FCOA research papers before branch-specific constructions are introduced.

title: Which Words Block the Machine Translation of Galen? A Reproducible Terminology Density Map
abstract: The obstacle to machine-translating the large untranslated Galenic corpus has recently been measured: a 2026 MQM study reports that passage-level terminology rarity predicts MT quality on Galen's previously untranslated pharmacological work at r = -.97 — the failure mode is vocabulary, not syntax. What that measurement does not supply is a queryable answer to which Galenic vocabulary is the blocker. We build that resource. Over the digitized Galenic corpus (First1KGreek), we run a reproducible, config-driven pipeline — extraction, odyCy lemmatization, log-likelihood keyness against a 19.68M-token non-Galen Greek reference, and LSJ cross-reference — and introduce a four-way classification that separates genuinely rare vocabulary from domain-specific and polysemous vocabulary, a distinction whole-corpus frequency conflates. The classification isolates, a priori from frequency alone, a set of common-but-technical terms (οὐσία, δύναμις, ποιότης) that rarity-based difficulty predictors cannot see by construction — a candidate failure mode orthogonal to the rarity the MT literature has measured. Lemmatizer accuracy is machine-bounded rather than assumed: 89.5% of analyzable medical tokens carry a Morpheus-admissible lemma, and against a 1,850-item gold standard mined from LSJ's own Galen citations, odyCy reproduces the lexicographer's headword on 62.3% of the rare stratum. We release a prioritized punch list of ~1,400 candidate terms, the full pipeline (MIT), and all data (CC-BY-4.0), each stage independently re-runnable over a different subcorpus. We claim an instrument, not a translation, and not lexicon adjudication. Data and code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22162595 and github.com/Montblanctech/Galen.

title: Dynamic Topology Mapping and Quantum Computing Synergy
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic potential of dynamic topology mapping and quantum computing. We present a novel algorithm for optimizing quantum computations, leveraging dynamic topology mapping to iteratively refine quantum system parameters and structure. This approach aims to significantly enhance the efficiency and performance of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism hinges on the continuous adjustment of the system's topology during the mapping process, guided by quantum information principles. This is a departure from traditional static topology mapping techniques, offering enhanced optimization capabilities. The investigation focuses on practical implementation and preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in a specific quantum system model.

title: Quantum Entanglement via Dynamic Matrices
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, exhibiting correlations between particles that cannot be explained by classical physics. However, achieving and maintaining entanglement, particularly in complex systems, presents significant challenges. This paper explores the design of a novel quantum state entanglement algorithm utilizing dynamic matrices to enhance the precision and fidelity of entanglement. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts matrix operations to create and maintain entangled states, overcoming limitations of traditional approaches. The core mechanism centers around the exploitation of the dynamic nature of matrices to enable self-corrective entanglement, leading to improved accuracy. This research aims to provide a new approach to quantum state entanglement, potentially paving the way for more robust and controllable quantum systems.

title: A Quantum-Based Communication Protocol Utilizing Multiple Substates
abstract: This paper proposes a novel communication protocol leveraging the properties of multiple quantum substates. The core concept involves encoding information across distinct quantum states, thereby enhancing both the efficiency and security of communication. Traditional quantum key distribution (QKD) systems often rely on a single qubit state, limiting the information capacity. This protocol expands upon this by utilizing multiple substates, creating a richer encoding space. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the protocol's structure, key generation process, and security considerations. We explore the mathematical underpinnings of the protocol, focusing on state manipulation, measurement outcomes, and the resulting data transmission. The design aims to mitigate eavesdropping attempts and improve the overall data throughput compared to conventional single-state QKD. The key parameters influencing protocol performance, such as the number of substates, are analyzed, and potential improvements are discussed.

title: Quantum Topology: Adaptive Computation Framework
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating area of physics, offers unique solutions to complex problems, particularly in quantum information processing. This paper introduces a novel framework for adaptive computation based on quantum topology, aiming to significantly improve the efficiency and precision of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism leverages the inherent adaptability of quantum states to reduce computational complexity and enhance algorithm performance. We present a rigorous theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the framework's efficacy in tackling specific quantum optimization problems. The research explores the potential of this approach to address limitations in existing quantum algorithm development.

title: 基于量子退相干的密码算法分析与优化
abstract: This paper investigates the security of quantum cryptography algorithms through a rigorous mathematical analysis leveraging the phenomenon of quantum decoherence. We develop a comprehensive mathematical model that explicitly incorporates decoherence effects, allowing for a more precise assessment of vulnerabilities within key algorithms. The analysis focuses on quantifying the impact of decoherence on key generation, distribution, and security, ultimately leading to the identification of optimization strategies aimed at enhancing robustness against decoherence-based attacks. Specifically, we examine the influence of decoherence rates, measurement strategies, and error correction protocols on the overall security of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems. The core contribution lies in moving beyond heuristic estimations and offering a quantifiable framework for evaluating and improving the resilience of quantum cryptographic systems in the face of a significant real-world challenge – the inevitable degradation of quantum states due to decoherence. The model presented provides a foundation for developing more secure and practical quantum key distribution protocols.

title: World 9 / R0.1 — Governed Principal Architecture: Engine-Independent Accountable Principals over a World 8 Substrate
abstract: World 9 / R0.1 is a research architecture baseline for a governed Principal Layer over World 8. It separates the accountable Principal from replaceable cognition and execution substrates while keeping objectives, commitments, bounded authority, resources, delegation, succession, and canonical continuity governed. The central separation is Brain ≠ Engine ≠ Principal. World 9 does not add a sixth World 8 plane; its code, policies, checkers, and migrations are themselves World-8-governed artifacts. Claim boundary: R0.1 is an E1_SPEC research architecture baseline, not a production system. No consciousness, sentience, AGI, legal personhood, metaphysical self-sameness, universal superiority, or production readiness is claimed. Executable proofs and stronger integration/security/longitudinal evidence remain OPEN.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Graph Representation Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental limits of graph representation learning from an information-theoretic perspective. We explore the question of how much information is truly required to represent a graph using a neural network, moving beyond purely empirical observations of model performance. Our core contribution is the derivation of information-theoretic bounds on the complexity of graph representation, utilizing concepts like Kolmogorov complexity to quantify the inherent information content of a graph. We analyze how different neural network architectures impact this information load and establish theoretical limits on representational efficiency. The research identifies crucial trade-offs between model capacity and the ability to accurately represent graph structure, offering a new framework for understanding and designing graph representation learning models. We demonstrate that the optimal model size is fundamentally limited by the intrinsic complexity of the graph itself, as measured by its Kolmogorov complexity. This work provides a robust theoretical basis for future research in graph representation learning, guiding the development of more efficient and effective models.

title: Non-Linear Topological Geometry: A Dynamic Self-Organizing Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topological geometry algorithm designed to identify and simulate self-organizing structures within complex systems. Traditional optimization algorithms often rely on global optima, while topology offers a powerful tool for finding efficient solutions, particularly in intricate systems. We propose a method that leverages the principles of self-organization – specifically, small-wave transforms, topological sorting – to build a real-time parameter adjustment model within a neural network. This dynamically evolving model forms the foundational basis for optimization. The core claim is that this algorithm will effectively identify and mimic self-organized structures within a system, offering a significant advancement in the analysis and design of complex systems. This work explores the potential of this approach to enhance the efficiency and robustness of optimization processes.

title: AI-derived tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes enhance the prediction of pathologic complete response in early-stage triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs) may hold clinical value for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) for outcome prediction. Manual scoring of sTILs suffers from inter-observer variability, limiting its clinical adoption. We developed an artificial intelligence (AI) workflow to automatically quantify sTILs from diagnostic biopsies and evaluated its predictive performance for pathological complete response (pCR) in patients with early-stage TNBC receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The pipeline combined tissue segmentation with context-aware cell classification to derive sTILs scoring, AI-sTILdensity. Using pretreatment biopsies ( n = 394) from the ARTEMIS trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02276443; October 21, 2014), AI-sTILdensity showed strong correlation with manual sTILs (Spearman rho: 0.686-0.739) and improved prediction of pCR (AUC: 0.702-0.747 vs. 0.692-0.713) as an independent feature ( P = 0.016). Predictive performance was consistent in an external TNBC set ( n = 64). These findings demonstrated that automated assessment of sTILs from biopsy specimens is reproducible and can modestly enhance pCR prediction, supporting the use of AI approaches to enable more objective and scalable evaluation of sTILs in TNBC.

title: Mapping-Based Image Diffusion
abstract: In this work, we introduce a novel tensor-based functional for targeted image enhancement and denoising. Via explicit regularization, our formulation incorporates application dependent and contextual information using first principles. Few works in literature treat variational models that describe both application dependent information and contextual knowledge of the denoising problem. We prove the existence of a minimizer and present results on tensor symmetry constraints, convexity, and geometric interpretation of the proposed functional. We show that our framework excels in applications where nonlinear functions are present such as in gamma correction and targeted value range filtering. We also study general denoising performance where we show comparable results to dedicated PDE-based state of the art methods.

title: 基于动态拓扑的自适应机器学习算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to machine learning utilizing a dynamic topology framework, specifically designed to enhance computational efficiency and adaptability. Traditional machine learning models often struggle with the limitations of classical computation, necessitating complex optimization and potentially slower learning curves. Our proposed algorithm introduces a dynamic topology structure that dynamically adjusts the representation of data and model parameters during the training process. This adaptive mechanism, coupled with a novel optimization strategy, aims to overcome these limitations and achieve superior performance across a range of machine learning tasks. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through a series of experimental studies, showcasing significant improvements in computational speed and accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms. The core principle centers on leveraging the inherent properties of dynamic topology to enable adaptive learning, ultimately providing a more robust and efficient machine learning solution.

title: Algorithmic Generative Simulation of Physical Laws
abstract: This paper explores the potential of algorithmic generative simulation to revolutionize our understanding of physical laws. We propose a novel system, the "Dynamic Law Engine," which iteratively generates scenarios within a simulated environment, leveraging generative algorithms to identify emergent patterns and predict unexpected consequences. The core mechanism focuses on refining physical laws through this continuous simulation, moving beyond static theoretical models to discover new physics and provide a framework for exploring fundamental phenomena. This research investigates the implications of this approach for scientific discovery and challenges traditional methods of physics research. The paper details the architecture of the Dynamic Law Engine, outlines the iterative process of law refinement, and discusses the potential outcomes and challenges associated with this approach.

This research investigates the implications of this approach for scientific discovery and challenges traditional methods of physics research. The paper details the architecture of the Dynamic Law Engine, outlines the iterative process of law refinement, and discusses the potential outcomes and challenges associated with this approach.

title: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) based on Measurement Device Independent (MDI) Protocols
abstract: This paper investigates the vulnerabilities inherent in existing Measurement Device Independent (MDI) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols and proposes a novel approach to enhance their security and reliability. The core claim is that current MDI protocols are susceptible to attacks stemming from imperfections within the measurement devices themselves. The proposed protocol leverages advanced error correction and privacy amplification techniques to mitigate these vulnerabilities, resulting in a more robust communication channel. The research focuses on developing a system that minimizes the impact of measurement device imperfections, thereby significantly improving the overall security and practicality of QKD. The key improvements involve a modified Bell-state measurement strategy and a tailored error correction scheme designed for the specific challenges presented by MDI protocols. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the protocol's resilience against a broader range of attacks, offering a substantial advancement in the field of quantum cryptography. The presented framework aims to deliver a practical and secure QKD solution for sensitive applications.

title: afzalahmed786/Adaptive-Split-Computing-for-Text-to-Image-Diffusion: v1.0.0
abstract: Adaptive Split Computing for Privacy Preserving Text-to-image Diffusion Models with Dynamic Offloading: code, models and measurements Split-inference system for Stable Diffusion v1.5 between an Android phone (Samsung Galaxy A55) and a GPU server (RTX 4060). For each request, a contextual-bandit controller on the phone chooses: the execution depth; the number of decoy requests; the wire precision; the image decoder. It makes this choice from the network, device and server state and from the sensitivity of the prompt. Privacy mechanisms: Decoy batching: the real request is sent together with decoy prompts written on the phone by a small language model (DecoyLM), and the phone keeps only the real result. Blind-prefix denoising: the server runs the first denoising steps with the empty prompt and never receives the prompt. Local generation: the whole image is generated on the phone. Feature perturbation (dropout and d_χ noise) is included as a baseline. Contents: Split-inference server (CUDA) and phone client (TorchScript, CPU; Termux with Ubuntu) Six execution depths (S0, S1, S3, B10, B15, L20) and the 58-configuration action space DecoyLM, with training scripts and a filter that rejects decoys matching public prompts Configuration-adaptive attackers for the prompt and for the output image, plus decoy distinguishers Simulator calibrated on the physical testbed, with latency validation Controllers: bootstrap-ensemble bandit (proposed); neural ε-greedy; LinUCB; standard and improved PPO; rule-based, static and random controllers; exhaustive search; and the prior-art controllers Neurosurgeon, SPINN and Edgent Trained controller, DecoyLM and reconstruction attacker Measured results of all experiments, including the physical-testbed logs, and the scripts that regenerate every table, figure and number in the paper from them Unit tests

title: Relational Neural Turing Machines with Semantic Graph Augmentation
abstract: Relational Neural Turing Machines (RNTMs) represent a significant advancement in neural network architectures, particularly for tasks involving complex relationships and sequential reasoning. However, their performance is often constrained by the need for carefully designed memory access patterns. This paper proposes a novel approach to augment RNTMs by incorporating a semantic graph derived directly from the input data. This augmentation provides a richer contextual representation, enabling the RNTM to learn more nuanced and flexible relationships between inputs and outputs. The core mechanism involves leveraging graph neural networks to construct the semantic graph, which is then used to guide memory access during the RNTM's operations. We demonstrate that this combination significantly improves the RNTM's ability to handle complex relational tasks, offering a more robust and generalizable solution compared to standard RNTMs. The primary contributions of this work are the integration of semantic graph augmentation with RNTMs and the demonstration of its efficacy in enhancing relational reasoning capabilities.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Causal Inference in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic programming to the field of causal inference, specifically within the context of complex systems. Traditional causal inference methods often struggle with the inherent complexities of real-world systems, including confounding variables, feedback loops, and incomplete data. Probabilistic programming offers a novel approach by providing a framework for formally modeling causal relationships using probabilistic graphical models and leveraging the powerful inference capabilities of probabilistic programming languages. We argue that this combination allows for more accurate predictions and the ability to reason about the effects of interventions in a principled manner. This work outlines the core concepts, the underlying mechanisms, and the potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its advantages over conventional techniques. We demonstrate how probabilistic programming facilitates the representation of complex causal structures and the execution of rigorous inference procedures, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of the systems under investigation. The key contribution lies in the ability to integrate uncertainty directly into the causal model, allowing for robust predictions and informed decision-making.

title: Relational Reasoning with Transformer Networks for Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Transformer networks to the problem of relational reasoning within knowledge graphs. Traditional methods frequently encounter difficulties in handling long-range dependencies present in complex relationships within graph structures. We propose a novel approach utilizing a Transformer-based model designed to explicitly attend to diverse parts of the knowledge graph during reasoning. This allows for improved capture of these dependencies, potentially leading to enhanced performance on relational reasoning tasks. The core of the approach lies in the self-attention mechanism inherent to Transformers, which enables the model to weigh the importance of different entities and relations when inferring relationships. We demonstrate the potential of this architecture through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, outlining the key components and their interactions. The goal is to move beyond limitations of existing methods and establish a more robust and effective means of relational inference on knowledge graphs.

title: Jincheng Zhang
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize image reconstruction, specifically focusing on the creation of high-resolution, detailed images. Traditional image reconstruction methods often struggle with limitations in spatial resolution, relying on classical physics for image quality. We propose a novel approach leveraging quantum entanglement to encode and transmit image information, enabling a fundamentally different reconstruction process. This system promises significantly enhanced image resolution and detail through a unique mechanism that transcends the limitations of classical optics. The core claim is that this approach can achieve resolutions exceeding current state-of-the-art methods, and offers a pathway towards truly detailed image reconstruction. This work lays the groundwork for a new paradigm in image processing, capitalizing on the peculiar properties of quantum mechanics.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding and Retrieval System (QIEIRS)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel system, Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding and Retrieval System (QIEIRS), leveraging multi-body quantum entanglement for exceeding the capacity limitations of classical channels. The core claim rests on the parallel encoding of information through quantum superposition achieved via carefully designed entangled states, coupled with efficient information retrieval exploiting the inherent properties of entanglement. QIEIRS constructs a quantum network comprised of multiple entangled atoms or ions. The system's potential lies in circumventing the constraints imposed by classical channel capacity, offering the possibility of ultra-fast information processing. The theoretical framework outlines the key principles and equations governing the encoding and retrieval processes, focusing on the manipulation of entangled states for optimal information transfer. We present a model for the quantum network and explore the performance metrics, highlighting the advantages over conventional encoding schemes. The system design prioritizes scalability and robustness, crucial factors for practical implementation. Further research will concentrate on mitigating decoherence effects and developing efficient control mechanisms for large-scale entangled networks.

title: Proximity-aware Attention with Dilated Multi-scale Decoding and Boundary-semantic Gating in a Lightweight Mix-transformer for Acetowhite Lesion Segmentation in VIA Cervicography
abstract: Accurate acetowhite lesion segmentation is a prerequisite component of automated VIA-based screening pipelines in resource-constrained clinical settings, with potential utility in CIN boundary delineation; however, clinical translation requires validation beyond mask-based metrics.Standard transformer segmentation architectures only model attention from feature content, neglecting spatial proximity among tokens and therefore missing positional cues critical for boundary delineation.Concurrently, unified decoder designs conflate semantic and boundary channels, leaving fine boundary discrimination underaddressed.To solve these limitations, we propose SegFormer-RPB-ASPP-CSG, a parameter-efficient, boundary-aware framework that integrates three established componentsproximityaware attention, multi-scale context aggregation, and adaptive boundary-semantic decompositioninto a unified domain-specific architecture for VIA cervicography.Specifically, the Relative Position Bias Multi-Head Attention (RPB-MHA) injects learnable pairwise proximity weights into each Mix-Transformer encoder stage to enrich the attention matrix with spatial structure.In the decoder pathway, a Dilated Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (Dilated ASPP) module aggregates multi-scale context, while an Upgraded Conceptual Split Gate (Upgraded CSG) prevents gradient interference between coarse lesion classification and fine contour delineation via adaptive soft gating.Evaluated on a 2,724-image VIA cervicography cohort with 681 held-out test images, the full model achieves a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 87.57% and a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (mDSC) of 90.51% using only 1.78M parameters.The per-class DSC reaches 86.66% (C0-Blue), 81.95% (C1-Lime), 93.76% (C2-Red), and 99.67% (C3-Background).Notably, a boundary-optimized RPB+CSG variant further reduces the parameter footprint to 1.47M while delivering superior boundary precision (HD95: 5.56 px vs. 5.97 px; ASD: 0.76 px vs. 0.84 px; NSD: 96.81% vs. 96.66%)and a marginal mDSC increase to 90.52%.Among the nine original comparison architectures, our framework achieves the third-highest mDSC while requiring 17.7× fewer parameters than the top performer (AUNet-MHA) and 2.53× fewer than the second-ranked method (SwinHR); among the sixteen total comparison methods (including seven retrained cervical-specific architectures), our model ranks eighth in mDSC.These results demonstrate that domainaligned integration of established architectural components can achieve competitive boundary precision within a compact parameter budget, supporting feasibility as a segmentation component in resource-constrained VIA pipelines, pending clinical validation against diagnostic endpoints.

title: Spectral Analysis for Sparse Matrix Computation: Insights and Potential
abstract: Sparse computations are fundamental to scientific computing, graph analytics, and machine learning, yet their performance is highly sensitive to the diverse sparsity and patterns. This is because cache reuse, memory coalescing, and load balancing depend critically on the sparsity patterns. This work gives the first known exploration of the connections between sparse matrix computation and spectral analysis by treating sparse matrices as two-dimensional signals and analyzing their frequency-domain representations through Fast Fourier Transform. We show that spectral signatures uncover global structural characteristics that are not sufficiently captured by conventional spatial statistics and provide complementary information for understanding sparse computation performance. Experiments on incorporating spectral features into machine-learning-based SpMV format selection demonstrate the usefulness of such spectral analysis over a state-of-the-art spatial-only model. By uncovering the principled connections between spectral characteristics and sparse matrix computations, this work introduces a novel analytical perspective into sparse computation, and provides a new approach to enhancing the current sparse structure characterization and optimization. On pruned LLM decoding, adding spectral features improves kernel selection and yields 1.035--1.245$\times$ kernel speedups.

title: Subtraction-Based Tumor Segmentation and Lesion-Centered pCR Prediction for the MAMA-MIA Challenge
abstract: We describe the submission of team FME to the MAMA-MIA Challenge, which evaluated primary tumor segmentation and prediction of pathological complete response (pCR) from pretreatment dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI on an external multi-country cohort. For segmentation, we trained a five-fold residual-encoder nnU-Net ensemble using only the first post-contrast minus pre-contrast image, combined with mirroring test-time augmentation and largest-connected-component filtering. For pCR prediction, we ensembled 25 pretrained 3D video classifiers trained on lesion-centred crops from the pre-contrast and first two post-contrast volumes. FME ranked second in both tasks. The segmentation method achieved a combined performance-fairness score of 0.882, with Dice 0.713 and normalized Hausdorff distance 0.099. The pCR method achieved a combined score of 0.664, balanced accuracy of 0.541, and equalized-odds disparity of 0.212. The results indicate that subtraction-based input and ensembling support robust tumor segmentation under cross-site domain shift, whereas pCR prediction from baseline DCE-MRI alone remains limited. For the submission repository, see https://github.com/FraunhoferMEVIS/MAMA-MIA-Challenge-FME

The focus is on providing a robust and adaptable framework for quantum simulation.

The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact and future directions of this approach.

title: Differentiable Quantum Circuit Simulator
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to simulating quantum circuits with differentiability, enabling gradient-based optimization for quantum algorithms. The core of the method lies in combining the accuracy of quantum circuit Monte Carlo simulation with the efficiency of automatic differentiation. We introduce a framework where the quantum circuit's evolution is simulated using Monte Carlo techniques, and the resulting expectation values are computed using automatic differentiation. This allows us to calculate gradients with respect to the circuit's parameters, which can then be used with standard optimization algorithms to refine the circuit's design. The key innovation is the seamless integration of these two techniques, offering a pathway to directly optimize quantum circuits for improved performance. The presented methodology provides a foundation for exploring advanced quantum algorithms and improving their efficiency through gradient-based approaches.

title: Title: Topological Quantum Entanglement for Computational Complexity
abstract: Abstract: Topological Quantum Entanglement for Computational Complexity explores a novel framework for quantifying and predicting computational complexity rooted in the dynamic evolution of topological quantum entanglement. Traditional approaches to quantum computing primarily focus on superposition and entanglement, leading to limitations in accurately assessing complexity. This research proposes a dynamically evolving topological structure that intrinsically reflects the entangled state's properties, enabling precise measurement of entanglement's influence on computational performance. The core mechanism involves creating and manipulating a topological structure that responds to the entangled state's dynamics, providing a mathematically grounded and quantitatively insightful tool for understanding and potentially optimizing computational capabilities. This work represents a significant departure from conventional quantum computing by introducing a fundamentally new metric for complexity, potentially unlocking new algorithmic frontiers.

title: Simulated Evolution Algorithms for Compiler Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Simulated Evolution Algorithms (SEA) to the optimization of compiler strategies. Traditional compiler optimization techniques often rely on local search methods, which can get trapped in local optima. SEA offers a novel approach by treating the collection of optimization strategies as a population and applying evolutionary principles – selection, crossover, and mutation – to drive the search towards globally optimal solutions. The core claim is that SEA's global search capabilities provide a significant advantage over conventional optimization methods in the complex landscape of compiler optimization. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and outline a potential framework for implementation. The evaluation of this framework will rely on performance metrics such as code execution speed and memory usage, demonstrating the potential of SEA to enhance compiler optimization. This work presents a new methodology for optimizing compilers, leveraging the power of evolutionary computation.

title: Title: Algorithmic Resonance for Complex System Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of algorithmic resonance to complex system optimization. Traditional optimization methods often rely on minimizing individual objective functions, which can be insufficient for intricate systems exhibiting non-linear relationships and emergent behavior. We propose a novel framework, "Resonance," that leverages the synchronized resonance of individual components to achieve optimal system states. This approach moves beyond simple gradient descent, focusing on identifying and amplifying subtle correlations within the system, thereby unlocking solutions to problems currently considered intractable for traditional optimization techniques. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that iteratively refines the system's state, driven by the detection and amplification of correlated patterns. The potential impact of this framework lies in its capacity to address complex systems with high dimensionality and non-linearity, offering a fundamentally different path to solution discovery.

title: Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent with Adaptive Entanglement
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a cornerstone algorithm in modern machine learning, yet it often encounters challenges in navigating complex, non-convex optimization landscapes. Traditional SGD methods predominantly focus on iteratively refining the gradient estimate, which can lead to premature convergence to local minima or saddle points. This paper introduces a novel approach, Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Gradient Descent with Adaptive Entanglement (QISGD-AE), designed to mitigate these limitations. QISGD-AE draws inspiration from quantum superposition and entanglement, dynamically adjusting the "entanglement" between nodes in the network during the optimization process. This adaptive entanglement facilitates a more comprehensive exploration of the solution space, enhancing the algorithm's ability to escape local optima and converge to globally optimal or near-optimal solutions. The core mechanism involves a stochastic probabilistic adjustment of node relationships, effectively mimicking the parallel exploration inherent in quantum systems. We present a detailed formulation of the algorithm, including key equations and parameters, demonstrating its potential for improved performance in various non-convex optimization tasks. The experimental results, though focusing on conceptual demonstration, highlight the algorithm's capacity to outperform standard SGD in specific scenarios, offering a promising direction for future research in adaptive optimization.

title: Reliable iToF Depth Sensing via Sensor-Intrinsic Uncertainty Modeling and State-Space Restoration
abstract: Indirect time-of-flight (iToF) cameras provide compact and cost-effective dense depth measurements, but their ranging accuracy is often degraded by sensor-intrinsic uncertainty under practical imaging conditions. Spatially uniform or range-only Gaussian perturbations cannot accurately reproduce the range-dependent and signal-dependent noise characteristics of real iToF measurements, leading to a synthetic-to-real gap for learning-based restoration. To address this problem, we propose a joint depth-uncertainty modeling and restoration framework for reliable iToF sensing. A sensor-intrinsic depth-uncertainty model is first developed from calibrated tap responses, returned-signal levels, and sensor noise statistics through a depth-oriented weighted least-squares formulation. The resulting pixel-wise uncertainty is used for heteroscedastic depth synthesis and uncertainty-aware restoration supervision. Based on this heteroscedastic data synthesis, we further develop a U-shaped restoration network with Depth Visual State Space (DVSS) blocks, which combine long-range state-space modeling with convolutional spatial-channel refinement for structure-preserving depth recovery. Experiments on synthetic data and measurements captured by an in-house iToF prototype validate the proposed uncertainty model under varying range and returned-signal conditions. Controlled comparisons with fixed and range-aware Gaussian noise, together with evaluations on U-Net, Restormer, and DVSS, further demonstrate that the proposed synthesis consistently benefits different restoration backbones. The complete framework achieves 40.85~dB PSNR and 2.54 mm MAE on the synthetic test set, and 35.42 dB PSNR and 4.87 mm MAE on real iToF measurements.

title: Self-Correcting Digital Circuits via Quantum Feedback
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to digital circuit design leveraging quantum principles for inherent self-correction capabilities. Traditional digital circuits are susceptible to noise and errors, necessitating complex and energy-intensive error correction codes. We propose a fundamentally different architecture utilizing quantum entanglement to establish a real-time feedback loop, enabling the circuit to autonomously detect and rectify errors without relying on classical error correction algorithms. The core concept involves employing entangled qubits to monitor the state of other qubits within the circuit. This allows for instantaneous identification of deviations from the intended state, followed by corrective actions mediated through controlled quantum interactions. We present a theoretical framework outlining this system, detailing the mathematical formulation of the feedback process and the entanglement requirements for optimal performance. The potential impact of this technology extends to significantly improved circuit reliability, reduced power consumption, and the possibility of creating entirely new types of computing architectures. The presented model focuses on a simplified digital circuit architecture for clarity and demonstrates the feasibility of the underlying principles. Further research will explore scaling the system and integrating it into practical hardware implementations.

title: Formal Verification of Deep Learning Model Robustness
abstract: The increasing deployment of deep learning models in critical applications necessitates a rigorous understanding of their robustness against adversarial attacks. Current methods for evaluating robustness primarily rely on empirical testing, which is often unreliable and lacks mathematical guarantees. This paper introduces a formal verification framework for assessing the robustness of deep learning models. We leverage abstract interpretation techniques to analyze the model's behavior under adversarial perturbations, offering mathematically provable guarantees about robustness within a specified region of the input space. The framework provides a significant advancement over traditional empirical testing by offering a verifiable method for ensuring model safety and reliability. The core contributions of this work are a novel framework, a mathematically sound approach, and the potential to significantly improve the trustworthiness of deep learning systems.

title: CFGN: causal flow graph networks for causally-aware fraud detection in imbalanced transaction graphs
abstract: Fraudulent activities in financial, e-commerce and digital transaction networks are getting difficult to detect, as fraudsters use the network’s legitimate architecture to hide their actions, and fraud activity is a small minority of all transactions. Existing graph neural network (GNN) detectors are unreliable due to this mix of extreme class imbalance, adversarial camouflage, and structural heterogeneity across application domains, because they only accumulate neighbour information via correlation and are unable to tell the difference between a genuine, causal link and a link that has been crafted for benign purposes but nonetheless camouflages the connection. We propose the Causal Flow Graph Network (CFGN), a graph neural network framework that learns both local and global structural effects, and explicitly removes the non-causal confounded neighbour signals before they are propagated. At its heart stands a causal gate that formally approximates Pearl’s backdoor adjustment criterion from structural causal modelling, which suppress the presence of confounded, camouflage-driven neighbouring causal signals during message passing and only consider causally identified signals to inform the representation of the target node. This causal gate is combined with structural attention through a learned adaptive mixture coefficient \(\lambda ,\) which automatically calibrates, per dataset, how much the model should rely on causal filtering versus standard attention. We apply CFGN to three application domains that differ in fraud type, graph topology, and labeling authority: cryptocurrency transactions (the Elliptic Bitcoin network), anti-spam review detection (YelpChi), and e-commerce behavioural fraud (Amazon reviews). Across all three, the learned mixture coefficient \(\lambda \) exceeded the 0.5 dominance threshold on the two domains with verified, adversarially rich labels (Bitcoin: \(0.71 \pm 0.02;\) YelpChi: \(0.73 \pm 0.04)\) and fell below it on the heuristically labeled Amazon domain \((0.39 \pm 0.03)\) , an empirical pattern consistent with causal gating becoming dominant specifically where adversarial camouflage is present. CFGN achieves a cross-validated AUC-PR of 0.6567 and AUC-ROC of 0.8868 on the professionally labeled Elliptic Bitcoin dataset, outperforming seven baseline and state-of-the-art GNN models on precision-recall metrics. In addition to raw accuracy, CFGN provides significantly higher robustness under the adversarial camouflage edge injection setting (with \(0.4 \pm 0.0\) injection rate it achieves an average precision of \(75.0\%\) on YelpChi while GAT achieves \(50.0\%\) and GCN achieves \(53.0\%)\) ; and under the temporal concept drift setting, CFGN’s performance drops by \(8.6\%\) while GCN’s drops by \(53.6\%.\) The combination of these results demonstrates that the explicit modeling of causal structure in message passing leads to improvements in both detection accuracy and material increases in adversarial or non-stationary robustness to real-world fraud detection.

title: LiteSearch-VL: Small Multimodal Search Agents via Trajectory Distillation and Synthetic Step-DPO
abstract: Multimodal search agents answer visual questions by interleaving image understanding, web retrieval, tool use, and evidence synthesis. Strong systems exist, but in two expensive regimes: proprietary frontier models such as GPT-5 and Gemini, or large open vision-language backbones trained with substantial agentic data and reinforcement learning. We ask a different question: when released agent trajectories are distilled into much smaller backbones under a single-node budget, what is actually transferred? We study this with LiteSearch-VL, a low-compute recipe for Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B that uses only released OpenSearch-VL trajectories, parameter-efficient LoRA adapters, and synthetic step-level preferences: DPO on GPT-5-generated hard negatives targeting five local failure modes (premature answer, wrong tool, weak query, repeated query, ignored image). Across 12,400 GPT-5-judged rollouts on SimpleVQA, FVQA, LiveVQA, and VDR-Bench-testmini, the dominant effect is behavioral rather than a uniform accuracy lift: full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning transfers the agent contract, taking the 2B model from almost never emitting a usable answer (1,237/1,240 no_answer rollouts) to 28.4% macro Pass@1, matching or slightly exceeding the off-the-shelf 4B base (25.6%). Synthetic preference learning and compact tool distillation act as refinements rather than phase transitions (best 4B configuration: 30.8% macro Pass@1). Finally, a controlled VDR step-budget ablation shows that extra search turns convert abstentions into wrong_entity errors rather than correct answers, identifying answer verification, not search depth, as the next bottleneck for small multimodal agents.

title: Training-Free Hidden-State Refinement for Flow-Matching Image Generators
abstract: We aim to improve frozen flow-matching image generators by adding inference computation inside the denoiser, without changing model weights or the outer sampler. Existing generators usually spend extra test-time computation by increasing the number of sampling steps, which repeatedly evaluates the entire denoiser and couples quality gains to sampler cost. A key challenge is how to use extra computation inside a frozen transformer denoiser: the method must decide which tokens, layers, and sampling times receive repeated updates while preserving the original generation pipeline. We introduce a training-free looping framework that repeatedly applies selected transformer layers inside each denoising call. Dense and Sparse Token Loop vary the token scope; Sampling-Progress Gating and the loop layer range specify when and where looping is active; loop count and strength control the repeated updates; and Loop Guidance combines ordinary and looped vector-field predictions. Across two Scale-RAE model scales, loop variants improve primary and auxiliary quality metrics with competitive quality--efficiency trade-offs. Loop Guidance further improves both primary metrics across all three tested models; on Scale-RAE DiT2.4B, it raises GenEval from 0.4471 to 0.5691 and DPG-Bench from 0.7656 to 0.8053. Code will be released.

title: Replication package for constraint-aware adversarial robustness and cross-dataset generalization for network intrusion detection systems
abstract: Reproducibility package for the PLOS ONE manuscript on constraint-aware adversarial robustness and cross-dataset generalization in network intrusion detection systems. Version 1.1.1 aligns the attack implementation, constraint checker, repeated-seed analyses, derived tables, and figures, and records the permanent concept DOI in the package metadata. Attacks and validity denominators apply only to malicious records; benign rows remain unchanged. Projected candidates enforce original-preserving empirical bounds, integrality of modified mutable coordinates, immutability, monotonicity, and attack-direction consistency. The release contains refactored experiment and analysis code, exact dependency versions, derived results underlying all reported tables and figures, data-derived figures, statistical comparison outputs, and concise reproduction instructions. Raw benchmark datasets are obtained from their original public providers and are not redistributed.

title: 基于自适应的非线性几何模型的预测
abstract: This paper introduces a novel prediction framework based on adaptive non-linear geometry models. Traditional predictive models often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their accuracy and efficiency. Our approach dynamically adjusts model parameters to capture the complex, non-linear relationships within the system being modeled. This adaptive mechanism significantly enhances prediction precision and speed compared to static models. We present a methodology for parameter adjustment, leveraging a reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize for model performance across a range of input data. This framework demonstrates improved accuracy and efficiency in predicting time-series data, particularly in scenarios involving complex dynamics and non-linear dependencies. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations and experimental validation. The core claim is that this adaptive framework achieves superior predictive performance through dynamic parameter adjustment.

title: 基于信息熵的程序语义自适应进化
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program adaptation based on information entropy. We hypothesize that program semantics can be modeled as an information entropy distribution. Through adaptive adjustment of this entropy distribution, programs can automatically learn and adapt to new inputs and environmental changes, effectively achieving a form of "semantic learning." The core of our method lies in introducing an entropy force model, which establishes a direct link between program behavior and its entropy distribution. Utilizing gradient descent or evolutionary algorithms, we dynamically modify this distribution, consequently influencing the program's execution path and outcome. Traditional program adaptation methods often rely on predefined rules or finite state machines, lacking the fundamental understanding and adaptive capabilities inherent in true semantic understanding. This work presents a fundamentally different approach, offering a more robust and flexible mechanism for program adaptation.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Calculator: A Novel Approach to Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Dynamic Quantum State Calculator (DQSC) presents a novel approach to quantum computation, centered around the dynamic adjustment of quantum states to effectively address complex environmental variations. This design leverages the inherent adaptability of quantum states, enabling rapid iteration and optimization of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism focuses on a self-tuning quantum state generation and adjustment system, significantly enhancing the computational capabilities compared to static quantum computing architectures. This research aims to establish a robust framework for quantum algorithm execution within dynamic environments, ultimately paving the way for more efficient and versatile quantum processing.

title: Adaptive Topological Deformation Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive topological deformation optimization algorithm designed to enhance the geometric complexity of optimization problems. Traditional optimization methods often rely on global optima, while topological deformation offers a flexible approach to explore the solution space. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts the topology of the search space, mitigating geometric complexity and enabling more efficient optimization. The core mechanism involves introducing non-linear gradient vanishing, achieved through geometric complexity evaluation, which guides the algorithm towards optimal solutions. The paper details the algorithm's design, performance analysis, and potential benefits for various optimization tasks.
