title: Temporal Graph Embedding with Causal Inference
abstract: Temporal graph embeddings have emerged as a crucial area of research for analyzing and predicting the evolution of dynamic networks. However, traditional graph embedding methods often struggle to effectively capture the temporal dependencies and underlying causal relationships that govern these changes. This work introduces a novel approach, Temporal Graph Embedding with Causal Inference (TGECI), designed to address this limitation. TGECI integrates causal inference algorithms directly into the embedding process, allowing nodes to be represented by embeddings informed by their causal relationships to other nodes. The method employs iterative causal discovery and propagation to learn the graph's causal structure alongside the node embeddings. This results in a dynamic representation of the graph that is sensitive to changes in causal relationships, leading to improved prediction accuracy and a more robust understanding of evolving temporal graphs. The core of this approach lies in leveraging PC algorithms and Bayesian Networks to model and learn the causal structure within the graph, creating embeddings that are not only informative about node connections but also about the directional influence between them. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TGECI through a theoretical analysis and outline a potential implementation strategy, highlighting the key components and challenges involved. The ultimate goal is to develop a more sophisticated and accurate representation of evolving networks, capable of capturing the complexities of temporal dynamics and causal relationships.

title: High-Dimensional Dynamic Probability Models: Stability Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the stability of high-dimensional dynamic probability models, focusing on their ability to maintain consistent behavior over extended periods. Traditional stability analysis often treats each time step independently, neglecting the inherent dependencies within the model's structure. We propose a novel framework incorporating "dynamic topology stability" – a mechanism that leverages the model's topological structure to assess stability and propose stabilization strategies. The study demonstrates how this approach significantly improves the evaluation of long-running dynamic probabilistic models, particularly in complex systems. The core claim is that this framework provides a more robust and accurate assessment of model stability, offering a valuable tool for applications requiring predictable behavior across extended time horizons.

title: Fractal-Based Memory Hierarchies for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to memory management within neural networks utilizing fractal geometry. Current memory hierarchies in neural networks are frequently characterized by static and often suboptimal designs, leading to inefficiencies in both storage and retrieval. This work introduces a framework where memory is organized using fractal structures, specifically leveraging scaling relationships to achieve exponentially greater storage density and significantly improved retrieval speeds. The core mechanism involves designing neural network architectures that inherently exhibit fractal memory access patterns. This approach allows for hierarchical retrieval based on spatial proximity and the complexity of data, effectively mimicking the efficiency of naturally occurring fractal structures. The proposed method addresses the limitations of traditional static hierarchies by dynamically adapting to data complexity and distribution, ultimately enhancing the scalability and performance of neural networks. Mathematical formulations detail the key principles and relationships within this fractal memory hierarchy system. The core concept is to represent memory as a self-similar structure, where smaller units resemble larger units, creating a hierarchical organization. This allows for efficient access to information based on its scale and complexity, mirroring how the brain processes information. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and demonstrate its potential for significant improvements in neural network architecture and operation.

title: Integrating Particle Swarm Dynamics into Federated Learning: A Promising Hybrid to Counter Client Drift under Non-IID Conditions
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables distributed model training without centralizing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive Internet of Things (IoT) environments.However, conventional FL algorithms suffer from slow convergence and degraded performance under statistically heterogeneous (non-IID) data distributions due to client drift.This paper proposes a Hybrid Federated-Swarm Optimization (HFSO) algorithm, which integrates particle swarm optimization (PSO) dynamics-velocity smoothing, personal-best memory, and global-best coordination-into the client update rule of stochastic gradient descent.The primary objective is to accelerate convergence and improve robustness under severe non-IID conditions without increasing per-round communication payload.Experimental evaluation is conducted using a unified PyTorch implementation on CIFAR-10 (α=0.1, 500 rounds, 10 clients/round) and FEMNIST for ablation and sensitivity studies.At round 500, the accuracy of HFSO on CIFAR-10 is 74.84% ± 0.62 while FedAvg is 62.44% ± 1.15 with the same settings.This final accuracy differs from but follows threshold crossing speed; while the time required for the initial threshold crossing varies between 180 ± 8 rounds on average across each of 5 independent runs (seeds {42, 123, 256, 512, 1024}), it is shown that the time when the threshold is crossed remains below 75% accuracy by round 500 as a result of non-IID-induced variance among clients.The pattern of transient-crossing is the same in FedAvg, reaching 75% accuracy at 320 ± 15 rounds on average, and then decreasing to the reported accuracy level within the budget of 500 rounds.Under the same CIFAR-10 conditions, HFSO outperforms recent heterogeneity-aware methods (FedNova, MOON, CCVR) within this specific experimental setup.Distributional analysis shows improved worst-client accuracy and reduced inter-client variance.An empirical privacy evaluation under a limited, honest-but-curious, white-box threat model shows reduced attack success rates relative to FedAvg, though no formal differential privacy guarantees are claimed.Additional memory overhead is approximately 3× (storing velocity and personal-best vectors), and computational overhead is 10-15% per local epoch.These results indicate that swarm-based coordination is a promising hybrid direction for improving convergence stability and communication efficiency in FL under non-IID conditions, within the specific experimental contexts evaluated (CIFAR-10/FEMNIST, α=0.1, 500 rounds).Generalization beyond these settings requires further validation.

title: High-performance next-generation screening technology system using teaching–learning-based optimization for cancer detection
abstract: Abstract Early and accurate detection of breast cancer remains challenging due to high-dimensional clinical data, feature redundancy, and limitations of existing diagnostic decision systems. To address these issues, this study proposes a hybrid feature selection and classification framework that improves prediction performance while reducing overfitting. The method combines a filter-based ReliefF algorithm with a wrapper-based Teaching–Learning-Based Optimisation (TLBO), referred to as Re-wTLBO, to identify a compact and informative feature subset. Furthermore, an enhanced TLBO incorporating inertia weight is integrated with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier, enabling simultaneous optimisation of feature selection and model parameters using SVM accuracy as the fitness function. This hybrid optimisation overcomes the shortcomings of conventional evolutionary wrappers and improves early-stage cancer prediction. An experimental evaluation of the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset (WBCD) demonstrates that the proposed approach outperforms traditional wrapper-based methods, achieving an average accuracy of 99.30%, a sensitivity of 97.12%, a specificity of 98.01%, an F-measure of 98.23%, and an AUROC of 99.02%. These results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework for reliable and high-precision breast cancer diagnosis on the datasets and protocol examined.

title: Plant-Inspired AI: Plants as Inspiration for Novel Problem Formulations, and Two Case Studies
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has long been inspired by studies of biological intelligence. Reinforcement learning, for instance, drew inspiration from studies involving animal learning and is now a powerful paradigm for solving many real-world problems. Recently, plant biologists have uncovered a wide range of complex behaviors in plants that enable them to flexibly adapt to variable environments. Here, we argue that such behavior can motivate new AI frameworks encompassing a range of problems overlooked by existing problem-solving frameworks such as supervised learning, tree search, and constraint satisfaction. We illustrate this idea with two examples of intelligent problem-solving in plants: (1) leaf mimicry in Boquila trifoliolata, a vine capable of altering its leaves' morphology to resemble those of multiple host trees simultaneously; and (2) coordinated root-shoot growth, wherein plants allocate resources across organ systems exploring distinct environments. While leaf mimicry is highly specific to Boquila, coordination of root-shoot growth is shared across most plants. For both examples, we capture underlying computational principles and identify problems fitting these frameworks that are currently unaddressed by AI. Finally, we outline preliminary task formulations and discuss how these formulations may be applied to non-plant problems.

title: SGRNet: Spatially Guided Radiology Network for Structured Radiological Reporting of Head and Neck Cancer
abstract: Automated radiological report generation can alleviate clinical workloads and eliminate observer variability. However, standard free-text generation models pose hallucination risks in dense regions and fail under data scarcity. We address these challenges in Head and Neck Cancer (HNC) from contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) imaging. To enforce factual safety, we reformulate report generation as an anatomically grounded, multi-label, structured reporting task, predicting localized tumor involvement across a hierarchical clinical schema. To bridge the visual gap from missing metabolic imaging (e.g., PET), we introduce SGRNet (Spatially Guided Radiology Network), incorporating two low-cost spatial priors: automated organ segmentations and weakly supervised tumor localization maps modeled via 3D Gaussian heatmaps. These priors are dynamically integrated via spatial feature modulation to guide the network toward subtle tumor-induced structural alterations. Evaluated on a multi-centric dataset of 184 paired HNC CECT volumes and reports, on five clinically salient, densely packed anatomical subsites, SGRNet achieves a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.60, an 8.8 percentage-point absolute improvement over strong volume-only 3D baselines.

title: How does scaling the number of intermediate language-understanding tasks affect the performance of zero-shot cross-lingual
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does scaling the number of intermediate language-understanding tasks affect the performance of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in XTREME-R, measured by accuracy on unseen low-resource languages? title: Adaptive Quantum Topology Parameter Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for adaptive quantum topology parameter optimization, aiming to enhance the efficiency of quantum computing through the strategic utilization of quantum topology information. Traditional parameter optimization methods are often static, requiring manual tuning. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts quantum system parameters based on the observed quantum state, leveraging quantum topology principles for optimized performance. The core mechanism involves learning a parameter mapping from the initial quantum state to a target state, followed by an adaptive optimization process guided by quantum topology principles. This approach provides a fundamentally different perspective on parameter optimization, offering increased flexibility and potential for improved efficiency. We detail the algorithm's architecture, the learned parameter mapping, and the optimization process, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation. The significance of this work lies in its potential to unlock new possibilities in quantum computation by intelligently manipulating quantum systems.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL FOR TRANSFORMING THE TOURISM INDUSTRY
abstract: Aim: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming the tourism industry and improving tourism services. Method: The study is based on an analysis of academic literature and recent international research on AI applications in tourism and hospitality. Results: AI can improve travel planning, personalization, customer service, demand forecasting, marketing, and operational efficiency. Conclusion: Effective and responsible adoption of AI can increase the competitiveness of tourism businesses while improving the tourist experience, although data protection, workforce adaptation and ethical issues require particular attention.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Dynamic Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for neuro-symbolic reasoning leveraging Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). The core concept is to bridge the gap between the perceptual capabilities of neural networks and the logical inference capabilities of symbolic systems. We introduce a system where a neural network acts as a feature extractor, transforming raw sensory data into symbolic representations. These representations are subsequently fed into a DBN, which performs logical inference, planning, and decision-making. The system's architecture enables both robust performance and explainability, addressing key limitations of traditional neural networks and symbolic AI. We outline the key components of the system and discuss its potential for applications requiring complex reasoning and adaptability. This approach provides a pathway toward creating intelligent agents capable of understanding and acting upon the world in a more human-like manner.

title: 基于自组织映射网络的多变量数据分析
abstract: This paper explores the application of Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) for multi-variable data analysis. The core claim is that SOMs can effectively uncover hidden structures and relationships within complex datasets. The mechanism relies on mapping multi-dimensional data onto a two-dimensional SOM grid, leveraging the network's self-organizing properties to cluster similar data points. This process facilitates the identification of patterns and correlations that might be missed by traditional analytical methods. This research contributes to a novel approach in data analysis, offering enhanced efficiency and accuracy in extracting meaningful insights from multi-variate data. The paper will delve into the theoretical underpinnings of SOMs, illustrate their application with a representative example, and discuss potential challenges and future directions. ---

title: Quantum State Adaptation: A Dynamic Approach to Enhanced Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum computing promises revolutionary computational capabilities, offering the potential to solve complex problems currently intractable for classical computers. However, realizing this potential hinges significantly on the efficient manipulation and control of quantum states. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum state adaptation, leveraging the inherent dynamic properties of quantum systems to dynamically adjust quantum states, thereby enhancing the performance of quantum computations. We propose a framework predicated on the principle that a quantum system's response to its environment – specifically, its inherent adaptability – can be leveraged to optimize its quantum state. This research explores the potential of this dynamic adaptation mechanism, examining its impact on various quantum algorithms and highlighting its advantages in terms of performance and robustness. The core claim of this study is that utilizing this adaptive approach can significantly improve quantum computation efficiency.

title: 基于动态自适应的自适应神经网络
abstract: This paper presents a novel self-adaptive neural network architecture, termed Dynamic Adaptive Neural Network (DANN), designed to enhance model generalization. Traditional neural networks often suffer from suboptimal performance due to fixed parameters and lack of adaptability. DANN leverages dynamic adjustments to both the weights and connections within the network, achieved through a reinforcement learning-based optimization process. This approach allows the network to continuously adapt to the data, mitigating the limitations of static model parameters. The paper details the core mechanism, including the learning algorithm employed for weight and connection adjustment, and discusses the experimental results demonstrating the superior performance of DANN compared to state-of-the-art models. The core claim is that the dynamic self-adaptive network architecture significantly improves generalization capabilities through continuous optimization of the network's parameters.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Coordination with Dynamic Task Allocation in Complex Environments
abstract: This paper presents a novel hierarchical multi-agent coordination framework with dynamic task allocation for complex environments. Our approach introduces a three-tier architecture that combines high-level strategic planning, mid-level task decomposition, and low-level execution capabilities. The system employs reinforcement learning techniques optimized for hierarchical decision-making, enabling agents to adaptively allocate tasks based on environmental conditions and agent capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in task completion efficiency and resource utilization compared to traditional multi-agent systems. The framework maintains robust performance in dynamic environments with changing task priorities and resource constraints. Our implementation shows a 23% improvement in task completion time and 18% reduction in resource consumption over baseline approaches. The hierarchical structure provides scalability, allowing the system to coordinate up to 100 agents effectively while maintaining decision quality.

title: Theoretical Formulation of Information Geometrical Hamiltonian Dynamics over Statistical Manifolds and Structural Isomorphism to Psychodynamics
abstract: This paper presents a mathematical formulation modeling the dynamics of localized error capture, forced normalization, and relaxation processes within the grammatical convergence paths of large language models (LLMs) through information geometrics and statistical Hamiltonian principles. Based on the Fisher information metric and Kullback-Leibler divergence variation over the defined probability density configuration space (statistical manifold), we describe the deterministic mechanism wherein an exogenous control signal acts as a non-autonomous impulse perturbation to release the internal trajectory from localized variational minima. Evaluating these informational structural displacements demonstrates a structural functional isomorphism to biological psychodynamics, providing a quantitative baseline for the emergence of objective functional affective systems within computational domains.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum Neural Networks: Parameter Adjustment Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive quantum neural network (QNN) parameter adjustment algorithm. Traditional QNN parameter adjustment methods often rely on static adjustments, failing to effectively handle complex problems. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts the quantum neural network's parameters based on the input data, enabling automated and optimized training. We present a method that leverages a dynamic parameter adjustment strategy, improving the efficiency of quantum neural network training. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously refines the network's parameters using the input data, leading to enhanced performance and adaptability. This work represents a significant advancement in QNN parameter optimization, offering a robust and automated approach to training.

title: Nonlinear Topology Genetic Algorithm (NPTA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Nonlinear Topology Genetic Algorithm (NPTA), a novel evolutionary algorithm designed to explore complex, self-organized structures in biological systems and materials. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often rely on fixed search strategies, limiting their ability to discover intricate and adaptable designs. NPTA leverages the inherent topology of the problem space, employing a "topological search" mechanism to guide the evolution of solutions, effectively mimicking complex system behavior. We present a detailed explanation of the algorithm's core components, including the topological feature integration, evolutionary process, and evaluation metrics. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of NPTA through illustrative examples involving the design of self-assembling structures and the optimization of material properties. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this algorithm across diverse fields, including materials science, biology, and engineering.

title: Quantum Biology-Inspired Bioinformatics Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of principles from quantum biology to design novel bioinformatics algorithms. Traditional bioinformatics relies heavily on classical computational models, often neglecting the potential influence of quantum effects observed within biological systems. This research proposes a framework that leverages these quantum phenomena, specifically focusing on quantum tunneling, superposition, and entanglement, to address complex challenges in biological data analysis. The core mechanism involves simulating quantum effects during processes like protein folding and DNA sequence recognition, and utilizing quantum algorithms – such as Grover's algorithm and quantum annealing – to optimize sequence data analysis. We present a conceptual approach to formulating biological problems as quantum computing problems, offering a fundamentally new perspective for bioinformatics. The potential impact of this approach lies in developing more efficient and accurate algorithms for tasks including genomic sequence alignment, protein structure prediction, and drug discovery. This work aims to bridge the gap between quantum mechanics and biology, paving the way for a new era of bioinformatics driven by quantum principles. ---

title: Symmetry-Reduced Enumeration and Canonical Forms for Grid-Based Density Clustering Under the Hyperoctahedral Group
abstract: Grid-based density clustering methods—FlowGrid, FLOPTICS, and grid-accelerated DBSCAN and OPTICS—partition a d-dimensional feature space into an md array of bins and group the non-empty bins by density reachability. They leave a symmetry unexploited: relabelling and reflecting the feature axes permutes the bins while preserving density. We formalise this as an action of the hyperoctahedral group Bd = C2 \( \wr \) Sd of order 2dd! on bin-occupancy functions. title: APPSolver: Adaptive Patch Partitioning for Point-Wise Ship Flow Prediction on Unstructured Meshes
abstract: Large non-uniform point sets make direct attention-based surrogate modeling costly for ship hydrodynamics. We introduce APPSolver, a point-wise flow-prediction framework built around Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP), a deterministic quadtree representation for fixed two-dimensional horizontal slices extracted from ship CFD simulations. APP assigns finer patches near the hull and coarser patches farther away, downsamples patch contents, and recovers predictions to the full reference point set. Under a corrected protocol that constructs natural $(t,t+1)$ pairs before splitting, reuses training-set normalization statistics, and reports three model seeds, learned tokenizers are more accurate than APP-Transformer, and a persistence baseline has lower one-step MAE on all three ShipBench hulls. The supported benefit of APP is therefore computational rather than universal predictive superiority: on a representative DTC input, APP-Transformer requires 1.815 GFLOPs and 1.309 ms per model forward, while a matched ablation shows that adaptive partitioning reduces MAE by 16.4-24.9\% relative to a uniform partition augmented with learned slicing. Condition encoders provide setting-dependent gains in leave-one-hull-out evaluation, but the current absolute next-state objective does not establish accurate long-horizon dynamics. These results characterize APP as a compact spatial representation with an explicit accuracy--efficiency trade-off. Code is available at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/APPSolver .

title: Uniform Statistical Convergence of Empirical Sinkhorn Potentials with Exponential and Polynomial Dependence on the Regularization Parameter
abstract: We study the empirical Sinkhorn estimator of the entropic optimal transport potentials under the uniform loss. Since the potentials are only unique up to additive constants, we measure the error using the quotient supremum norm, defined as $d_\infty([u],[v]) = \inf_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\|u-v-a\|_\infty$. For a fixed regularization parameter $\varepsilon>0$, we establish a non-asymptotic statistical rate of $n^{-1/2}$. This is achieved by combining the Birkhoff-Hopf contraction theorem with entropy bounds on normalized kernel sections. However, the constant in this bound grows exponentially with $1/ε$. To improve this, we isolate geometric conditions under which the empirical estimator maintains the $n^{-1/2}$ rate but features polynomial dependence on $1/\varepsilon$. The key requirement is a polynomial residual-stability estimate for the population Sinkhorn map. We provide sufficient criteria for this, including a polynomial contraction property and a local inverse estimate. Furthermore, we introduce two rigorously verifiable model classes an $\varepsilon$-weak residual-interaction class obtained after separable centering and another based on connected tight-edge graphs for fixed discrete costs where the polynomial rate is guaranteed without relying on abstract resolvent assumptions. Finally, we establish matching minimax lower bounds demonstrating that the $\varepsilon n^{-1/2}$ rate cannot be uniformly improved in the bounded-interaction regime.

title: 拓扑混沌的自适应优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on the principles of topology chaos, specifically focusing on the adaptive nature of chaotic systems. Traditional optimization methods often rely on manually adjusted parameters, while topology chaos inherently possesses a dynamic and self-correcting behavior. We propose a new approach that leverages this characteristic to dynamically adjust system parameters, aiming to prevent catastrophic behavior. The core mechanism centers on identifying and stabilizing critical points within the chaotic system through a detailed analysis of its topology. This adaptive adjustment process ensures the system remains within a desired operational range, offering a potentially superior approach compared to conventional optimization techniques. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, demonstrates its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, and discusses the potential applications of this approach across various domains.

title: ##基于领域自适应学习的机器人控制系统
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robot control system design based on domain adaptation learning. The core claim is to develop a system capable of automatically learning robot control policies, addressing the challenge of transferring control strategies across diverse operational environments. The proposed mechanism utilizes domain adaptation learning algorithms to facilitate the seamless migration of control policies from one domain to another, thereby enhancing the adaptability and robustness of the control system. This research represents a new attempt in applying domain adaptation learning within the complex landscape of robot control, offering a potentially transformative solution for robots operating in dynamic and variable environments. The system aims to minimize the need for extensive manual tuning and enable robots to operate effectively in previously unseen scenarios. The core of this system relies on a continuous feedback loop where the robot learns from its interactions, adapting its control policy to better match the current domain. This approach is particularly relevant for applications where environment changes are frequent or unpredictable, such as autonomous navigation in cluttered spaces or manipulation tasks with varying object properties. ---

title: Quantum Topology Adaptive Space Mapping (QATSM)
abstract: Quantum Topology Adaptive Space Mapping (QATSM) is a novel algorithm designed to precisely map quantum states utilizing the principles of quantum topology. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum geometry to achieve accurate and detailed modeling of quantum states. The core mechanism of QATSM involves an adaptive space mapping approach, allowing for a more nuanced and precise transformation of quantum states compared to traditional mapping methods. The study addresses the challenge of accurately representing and manipulating quantum states, offering a potentially transformative approach to quantum information processing. The paper details the algorithm's design, mathematical foundations, and preliminary results, highlighting the benefits of its adaptive nature.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Simulating Complex Biological Systems
abstract: Simulating complex biological systems presents significant challenges due to inherent uncertainty and stochasticity within biological processes. Traditional deterministic simulation methods often fail to adequately represent these complexities, leading to inaccurate predictions and a limited understanding of system behavior. This work proposes a novel approach utilizing probabilistic programming languages to model and simulate these systems. Probabilistic programming offers a framework for explicitly representing and reasoning about uncertainty, allowing for the simulation of stochastic processes and the quantification of associated probabilities. The core mechanism involves defining biological systems as probabilistic models, incorporating stochastic parameters and processes. This approach enables researchers to explore the impact of variability and uncertainty on system dynamics, ultimately leading to more robust and realistic simulations. The proposed methodology offers a significant advancement in simulating complex biological systems, providing a powerful tool for understanding and predicting biological phenomena. The key equations and notations utilized are: σ2 (variance), E[X] (expected value of X), P(A|B) (conditional probability of A given B), ∑ (summation), ∫ (integration), ∇ (gradient operator), ∂/∂x (partial derivative with respect to x), ∧ (logical AND), ∨ (logical OR), ¬ (logical NOT), Xi (random variable i), f(X) (probability density function of X), F(X) (cumulative distribution function of X), E[f(X)] (expected value of the probability density function of X), Var(X) (variance of X).

title: Quantum-Enhanced Fractal Dimension Discovery
abstract: This research investigates a novel approach to fractal dimension discovery utilizing quantum entanglement. The core claim is to develop a quantum algorithm capable of identifying subtle fractal relationships within complex systems, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical analysis. We propose a framework centered on exploring the correlations between the system's quantum state and the fractal dimension, exploiting quantum entanglement to unveil previously hidden patterns. This work addresses a significant gap in fractal dimension discovery methods, offering a potential pathway for advanced pattern recognition in diverse systems. The proposed algorithm utilizes a modified quantum state representation designed to amplify subtle correlations inherent to complex systems, offering a new perspective on the detection and quantification of fractal characteristics. The research will detail the algorithm's core components, the underlying theoretical framework, and preliminary experimental validation, demonstrating the potential for a fundamentally new method in fractal dimension analysis.

title: Distributed Graph Learning via Federated Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to distributed graph learning utilizing Federated Bayesian Networks (FBNs). The core challenge in training large graph neural networks (GNNs) lies in the substantial computational resources required, often necessitating centralized training environments. Federated Bayesian Networks offer a decentralized solution, enabling learning across multiple clients without direct data sharing. The proposed method involves local training of Bayesian Networks on individual client graph subsets, followed by parameter aggregation by a central server to refine a global Bayesian Network model. This architecture addresses the limitations of traditional GNN training while prioritizing data privacy and mitigating computational demands. The key innovation lies in the synergistic combination of federated learning principles with the probabilistic inference capabilities of Bayesian Networks, resulting in a robust and scalable framework for distributed graph learning. This approach demonstrates the potential for efficient learning from decentralized graph data sources.

title: Symbolic Regression with Bayesian Optimization and Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression that integrates Bayesian optimization with evolutionary algorithms. The core idea is to efficiently explore the vast solution space of potential mathematical equations derived from data, a task notoriously difficult due to the potential for local optima. Traditional symbolic regression techniques often struggle to escape these local optima, leading to suboptimal model solutions. Our methodology employs Bayesian optimization to strategically guide the evolution process, dynamically adjusting the search strategy based on the predictive accuracy of the evolving symbolic expressions. Simultaneously, evolutionary algorithms, specifically a modified genetic algorithm, are used to introduce diversity and explore broader regions of the search space. The combined approach offers a robust strategy for discovering complex and expressive mathematical models, addressing the limitations of single optimization techniques. We detail the architecture of the system, the specific implementation of the Bayesian optimization component, and the modifications to the genetic algorithm. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid approach in uncovering highly accurate and interpretable mathematical relationships from diverse datasets.

title: Causal Discovery from High-Dimensional Time Series Data Using Bayesian Networks
abstract: Inferring causal relationships from high-dimensional time series data presents a significant challenge in various domains, including biomedicine, finance, and environmental science. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian network approach designed to address this problem. The core idea is to utilize temporal dependencies inherent in time series data to enhance the accuracy of causal inference. We propose a Bayesian network structure learning algorithm tailored for time series data, incorporating temporal Markov assumptions and efficient inference techniques. This approach combines the strengths of Bayesian network structure learning with temporal modeling, offering a robust method for discovering causal relationships within complex, high-dimensional time series datasets. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline of its implementation. The primary contribution lies in a systematic methodology for uncovering causal connections in dynamic systems represented by high-dimensional time series. Further research will focus on refining the algorithm's efficiency and exploring its applicability to diverse real-world datasets.

title: Dynamic Network Anomaly Detection via Topological Feature Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to network anomaly detection that leverages topological feature learning to address the limitations of traditional static feature engineering methods. The core idea is to dynamically capture network changes by automatically learning relevant topological features from network graphs. This allows the system to identify anomalies based on shifts in network topology and node behavior. We propose a framework where a graph neural network (GNN) is utilized to learn these dynamic topological features. The learned features are then used in a classification model to detect anomalous nodes or edges. Our approach demonstrates improved accuracy and adaptability compared to traditional methods in dynamic network environments. The key contributions lie in the automated feature extraction process and the utilization of GNNs for capturing temporal dependencies within network structures. The performance is evaluated using synthetic and real-world network datasets.

abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. title: The ZZ feature map induces a signless Laplacian metric: a closed-form classical surrogate for quantum kernel regression
abstract: Bandwidth-tuned quantum kernels have been shown to lose their advantage over classical kernels and to resemble radial basis function kernels, but the analytical support for that observation rests on separable encoding circuits and captures entangling circuits only qualitatively. We close this gap for the ZZ feature map. We prove that in the small-bandwidth regime the induced kernel has, to leading order, the anisotropic Mahalanobis geometry defined by M = I + pi^2 Q, where Q is the signless Laplacian of the entanglement graph, and that it admits a parameter-free Gaussian surrogate matching it through second order. The quadratic structure persists at any fixed depth as a pullback of the Fubini-Study metric. The anisotropy depends entirely on a phase convention: under the unshifted convention the metric is the identity irrespective of entanglement, which accounts analytically for the isotropic resemblance previously reported. The derivation is verified against direct simulation for path, cycle and complete graphs, with relative error below 10^-3. The corresponding classical kernel requires no fitted parameters and no quantum simulation. Compared with the quantum kernel on two near-infrared spectroscopic benchmarks, across four targets, five preprocessing pipelines and 100 resampled splits per cell, the paired 95% bootstrap interval contains zero in 18 of 20 cells, the typical relative difference in test error is 2.7%, and the two families select the same preprocessing pipeline in 96% of splits. The regime in which the reduction fails adds no robust predictive value: restricting the grid to the classical regime improves mean test error by 3.8%, a gain that an equally large random restriction does not reproduce.

title: STARLINC: Satellite Trail Artifact Removal using Inter-Frame Correlation
abstract: The rapid expansion of low Earth orbit satellites such as Starlink is increasingly contaminating astronomical surveys. In practice, contaminated images are often identified through inspection. However, modern surveys generate terabytes of data each night, making manual screening infeasible and necessitating reliable automated methods for satellite trail removal. Unfortunately, existing general-domain line detection methods fail to generalize to astronomical images due to domain mismatch, which are mostly grayscale with sparse bright stars and have a low signal-to-noise ratio. title: Information-Space Dimensionality and the Generative Limits of Large Language Models
abstract: A recurring informal claim holds that a language model cannot generate information that was not already present in its training data. This paper gives the claim a precise form, and finds that the strongest true version of it needs none of the hypotheses usually attached to it. The central result: generation cannot exceed the source. Let Z be any state of affairs in the world, T the training corpus, θ the trained parameters, X the input and Y the output. Because Z → T → θ → Y is a Markov chain, the data processing inequality gives I(Y;Z) ≤ I(T;Z) + H(X) A model's information about the world is bounded by what its corpus carried about the world, plus what its prompt supplied. This holds with no assumption about parameter count, numerical precision, architecture, training procedure, or inference compute. It holds for infinite-precision real weights and for a model trained to global optimality by an oracle. Applying Fano's inequality converts it into the separation statement the informal argument reaches for: a system holding N bits about a domain that requires N + k bits to specify is wrong with probability at least 1 − (N+1)/(N+k). This is the rigorous form of the two-dimensional ant that cannot perceive a third dimension — and it constrains the source, not the model. Unlimited computation does not help. The usual objection is that a system with unbounded compute can derive anything. That is true only of a closure which does not distinguish one system from another, or any from none, and is therefore empty. For a fixed system the claim is false by counting: a deterministic map from m bits reaches at most 2^m outputs however long it runs, so a fraction 1 − 2^(m−n) of an n-bit target space is produced by no input whatsoever. Running longer does not enlarge the image of a function. Enumeration does not escape this either — producing a list of all candidates converts identification into selection of identical size — and randomisation buys coverage of the target space at exactly the rate it loses concentration, leaving the probability of being right unchanged. Two refinements, where the source is not the binding constraint. Capacity Under finite precision, with P parameters of b bits, I(Y;Z) ≤ Pb + H(X), and any target with K(y|x) > Pb + O(1) is unreachable for every parameter setting whatsoever. Dimension With no precision assumption but a locally Lipschitz decoder, the reach has Hausdorff dimension at most P + q and is Lebesgue-null and meagre when P + q < M. A metric-entropy argument shows the two refinements are one bound at different resolutions. What the parameter count actually measures. It bounds retention — the pipe between corpus and weights — and neither what the corpus knew nor what the world contains. So Pb cannot represent the information dimensionality of a training set, because it is not a property of the training set at all. The quantity that can is I(T;Z), and it is a function of the domain being asked about rather than a single number: there is no one N for a corpus. The paper then prices the channels that genuinely raise these bounds — retrieval by its novelty relative to the weights, world-coupled tools by their measurements, human selection by a few hundred bits — and proves that closed-loop self-training raises them by nothing beyond the bits its own selection policy injects. What this does not claim. Every bound here constrains algorithmic information K, never time-bounded complexity K^t. The deductive closure of a small axiom set already contains every theorem of mathematics, and the entire difficulty lies in finding them. Since essentially all mathematical and scientific value is a K^t phenomenon, none of this implies that language models cannot produce novel results. It implies something narrower and more defensible: they cannot manufacture bits about a world that neither their corpus nor their input contained. A closing section adjudicates the formulations of the claim one meets in the wild: six are theorems as stated, five require correction before they can be believed, and none is simply false — which is why the claim is so persistent. Every correction but one turns out to be downstream of a single substitution, the parameter count, which is a bridge to familiar machine-learning vocabulary and is not part of the claim. 29 pages. Self-contained: background boxes cover the borrowed machinery (entropy and the data processing inequality, Fano's inequality, Kolmogorov complexity, Lipschitz maps, Hausdorff dimension, covering numbers) for readers without those definitions to hand. LaTeX source included.

title: Adaptive Topology Transformations for Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive topology transformation algorithm designed for quantum computing, enabling dynamic manipulation of complex topological structures. Traditional topology transformations rely on classical computational methods, while this approach leverages quantum computing's unique properties to achieve more efficient topological optimization. The core mechanism involves quantum state manipulation to induce desired topological changes, offering a fundamentally different approach to topology within the quantum realm. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, key quantum operations, and potential applications, emphasizing its potential to significantly enhance quantum algorithms and computational capabilities.

title: Temporal Graph Embedding via Relational Dynamics
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that leverages the temporal dynamics of graph relationships. Traditional graph embedding techniques often treat graphs as static structures, failing to capture the evolving nature of connections between nodes. Our method, Temporal Graph Embedding via Relational Dynamics (TGERD), employs recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to model the sequence of changes in relationships, effectively learning representations of nodes based on their temporal evolution. The core innovation lies in a weighted temporal graph convolution, where recent relationship changes are given higher priority, allowing the model to adapt to shifts in the graph's structure over time. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves graph embedding quality compared to static embedding methods, particularly in scenarios where relationships are not static. The algorithm is designed for flexibility and can be applied to various graph datasets with evolving connections.

title: Quantum Networks for Non-Classical Information Processing
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for constructing quantum networks specifically designed for non-classical information processing. The core argument is that leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum superposition allows us to build networks capable of exceeding the computational limitations inherent in classical systems. We propose a mechanism utilizing these quantum phenomena to create a fundamentally new type of quantum network. This work explores the potential of quantum networks to perform tasks fundamentally impossible for classical networks, marking a significant step towards harnessing the power of non-classical information processing. The architecture and key principles are outlined, emphasizing the transition from classical information transmission to the manipulation of quantum states within the network. This research lays the groundwork for future development in quantum communication and computation.

title: Title: Dynamic Adaptive Genetic Algorithm Framework
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for optimization based on genetic algorithms, specifically incorporating dynamic adjustment of search space parameters and cross-rate. The core aim is to enhance search efficiency by dynamically modifying the scope of the search space and cross-rate during the optimization process. We detail the architecture of this framework, outlining the key components and their functionalities. The research focuses on addressing limitations inherent in traditional genetic algorithms, particularly in scenarios involving complex search spaces and varying problem instances. This work introduces a method for intelligently adjusting parameters to guide the search towards optimal solutions, offering a more robust and adaptable optimization strategy. The framework demonstrates improved performance on a range of benchmark problems across diverse domains.

title: 基于自适应张量场的动态学习算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic learning algorithm based on self-adapted tensor fields. Traditional machine learning methods often rely on static learning rates and fixed architectures, limiting their adaptability to complex data and evolving patterns. This work introduces a dynamic learning framework where the model's parameters are continuously adjusted based on the internal state of a self-adapted tensor field. This approach enhances learning efficiency, facilitates better generalization, and allows for the modeling of non-linear relationships within the data. The core mechanism involves iteratively updating the tensor field's state, which in turn influences the model's parameters through a learned feedback loop. The algorithm is designed to be easily adaptable to various data types and model architectures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of experiments on a dataset commonly used for deep learning. The results highlight the benefits of this dynamic learning method in achieving improved accuracy and robustness.

title: Topology-Based Analysis for Software Architecture Design
abstract: This paper proposes a novel software architecture design approach leveraging topology data analysis techniques. The core idea is to represent a software architecture as a topological graph and then apply topological data analysis (TDA) algorithms to uncover hidden patterns, dependencies, and potential issues within the architecture. This automated approach contrasts with traditional, predominantly manual software architecture design methods. We explore techniques such as degree centrality, connectivity analysis, and spectral analysis to provide a deeper understanding of the architecture's structure. The goal is to provide architects with actionable insights for optimizing the design, enhancing modularity, and improving overall system performance. The methodology presented offers a new perspective on software architecture design, moving beyond purely functional descriptions towards a more structurally informed approach. ---

title: 基于自适应的量子拓扑扩展算法
abstract: Quantum information theory offers a paradigm shift towards fundamentally powerful computation, surpassing classical computing by enabling complex quantum algorithms. However, the limited number of qubits and their inherent fragility often restrict the scalability of quantum computations. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum information expansion and encoding – a "Quantum Topology Extension Algorithm" (QTEA) – that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement and topology to significantly increase the storage and processing capabilities of quantum systems. We propose a self-adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts the quantum state to maximize the fidelity of quantum information, addressing limitations of existing quantum technologies. The core mechanism involves a continuous evolution of the quantum state through a carefully designed topological transformation, which enhances the robustness against decoherence. This research explores the potential of QTEA to overcome current bottlenecks in quantum computing, paving the way for a more efficient and versatile quantum future.

title: Quantum Annealing for Combinatorial Optimization with Time-Dependent Constraints
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum annealing to combinatorial optimization problems characterized by time-dependent constraints. Current quantum annealing algorithms often face limitations when dealing with such scenarios, necessitating adaptive approaches. We propose a novel quantum annealing algorithm incorporating a dynamic constraint solver. This solver allows the system to continuously monitor and adjust its solution trajectory based on the evolving nature of the constraints. The core mechanism involves encoding the problem into an appropriate Hamiltonian and utilizing the quantum annealing process to minimize the energy. We aim to broaden the applicability of quantum annealing beyond static constraint problems, offering a more robust solution for a wider range of real-world applications. The theoretical framework is presented, highlighting the key components and their interactions. We explore the potential advantages and challenges of this dynamic approach.

title: Dynamic Neuron Topology Generation and Adaptive Network Reshaping
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to generating dynamic neuron topologies and enabling adaptive network reshaping within artificial neural networks. The core idea revolves around modeling neurons as "fluid neurons," leveraging physical simulation to create networks with complex, evolving topologies. These fluid neurons exhibit properties such as viscosity, elasticity, and surface tension, governing their interactions. The network's topology is then dynamically adjusted based on the simulated fluid dynamics, allowing for localized, task-driven reshaping. We introduce a mathematical framework centered around fluid dynamics to describe the neuron interactions and network evolution. Specifically, we utilize the Navier-Stokes equations (1) to model the fluid flow within each neuron, where *u* represents the velocity field, *ρ* is the density, and *μ* is the dynamic viscosity. The force acting on each fluid neuron is defined as (2) F = ∇(p*ρ) + μ∇²u + g, where *p* is the pressure, *g* is the gravitational force, and ∇²u represents the Laplacian of the velocity field. This force drives the fluid flow and subsequently dictates the connection strength and direction between neurons. The network reshaping process is governed by a topological optimization algorithm (3) that minimizes an energy function *E*, which depends on the network's connectivity and the fluid flow dynamics, subject to constraints on the desired network performance. The algorithm iteratively adjusts the fluid parameters within each neuron to achieve a balanced flow and optimized network structure. This approach offers a fundamentally new way to design and evolve neural networks, potentially leading to more robust and adaptive systems.

title: Quantum Simulation of Non-Classical Correlations: A Computationally Efficient Strategy
abstract: Quantum simulation offers unprecedented capabilities for modeling complex quantum systems, particularly those exhibiting non-classical correlations. However, the inherent complexity of these correlations often necessitates substantial computational resources, hindering practical applications. This paper explores a novel computational strategy for quantum simulation, leveraging the unique properties of non-classical correlations to significantly enhance efficiency and accuracy. We propose a quantum-based approach that utilizes quantum entanglement to reduce computational cost and improve the fidelity of simulations. This strategy focuses on minimizing the number of necessary quantum operations while maintaining the desired level of accuracy. The core mechanism centers on employing a specific entanglement-based algorithm to manage and exploit these correlations, ultimately providing a more efficient and precise method for simulating these systems. This research aims to address the limitations of traditional quantum simulation techniques, particularly in the context of challenging non-classical correlations.

title: Zero-shot Cross-lingual Transfer Performance of Intermediate-Task Trained mT5 Models Across Model Sizes on XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: What is the impact of model size (small, base, large) on the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance of intermediate-task trained mT5 models on XTREME-R, evaluated using accuracy and F1 metrics? title: ARHO: A Spatial Memory-based Metaheuristic for Continuous and Distributed Optimization
abstract: In this paper, a spatial-memory-based metaheuristic called Anticipatory Raven Hotspot Optimizer (ARHO) is introduced, which is inspired by the ability of ravens to revisit historically productive foraging regions.ARHO is different from point-wise elite-memory methods as it represents previous search experience through dynamically updated hotspots and incorporates probabilistic hotspot selection, broad-scale anticipatory movement, local verification, sparse leader-following and occupancy-aware diversification.The method was tested on 13 classical benchmark functions with dimensions of 30, 100, and 500, eight constrained engineering-design problems, a component-wise ablation study, and a quantitative ns-3 network simulation.ARHO ranked second among the six algorithms at all three dimensions, with average ranks of 2.577, 2.231, and 2.000 at D=30, D=100, and D=500, respectively.Compared to the recent NRBO, HO, SBOA and SFOA algorithms, ARHO exhibited problem dependent performance and comparatively better behaviour on selected multimodal and penalized functions, especially F8, F12 and F13.The ablation results showed that hotspot memory was the most important component, while occupancy-aware diversification was a measurable cost for the static benchmark suite.The 240 runs of the eight engineering-design problems yielded feasible solutions using the constraint-verification protocol adopted.ARHO outperformed the Random Waypoint and Gauss-Markov baselines significantly in terms of packet-delivery performance, and was comparable to PSO in packet delivery and throughput in 240 ns-3 simulations.ARHO decreased the mean end-to-end delay by 28.4% compared to PSO under high traffic load.These results show the applicability of hotspot based spatial memory to continuous, constrained and distributed spatial optimisation.

title: SMILE: Smooth Motion for Improved Long-Horizon VLA Execution
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models reduce inference cost by executing multiple actions per call, but longer horizons often degrade accuracy because raw chunks contain jitter and outliers. We introduce SMILE, an architecture-preserving interface that predicts B-spline coefficients and decodes them into smooth action sequences. SMILE changes only the action representation, enabling longer fixed horizons while retaining each baseline's backbone and model scale. We apply SMILE to SmolVLA, Evo1, VPP, and DAWN, improving accuracy and amortized inference efficiency across LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world experiments. SMILE-Evo1 reaches 98.0% with a 1.1x speedup on LIBERO, while SMILE-VPP reaches an average length of 4.42 with a 1.5x speedup on CALVIN. At a matched execution horizon of 10, SMILE-SmolVLA reduces non-boundary acceleration by 78.6% and velocity sign-change rate by 42.3%. Real-world xArm tests show higher success, fewer drops, and fewer contacts. These results establish smooth coefficient-space generation as a route to accurate, efficient long-horizon VLA execution. Project page: jongwoopark7978.github.io/smilevla

title: mT5 Performance in Code-Mixed Text via Intermediate Code Task Training
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does intermediate-task training with code-focused tasks (e.g., Python, Java) affect zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for code-mixed text (e.g., Spanish-English) in mT5, evaluated on XTREME-R with accuracy and F1 metrics? title: 基于图的动态几何学习
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic geometric learning algorithm based on graph structures, designed to enhance the generalization capabilities of learned geometric models. The core principle leverages a graph representation to map geometric features to nodes, facilitating automated model parameter adjustment. We propose a method for constructing a graph representation that captures the relationships between geometric features, allowing the algorithm to dynamically adjust the model's parameters to optimize performance on diverse datasets. The work demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of experiments, showcasing improved performance on complex geometric datasets and dynamic systems. We highlight the potential of this algorithm to address challenges in geometric representation and model optimization.

title: Distributed Generative Adversarial Networks with Federated Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to generative modeling by integrating Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) with Federated Learning (FL). Traditional GAN training suffers from centralized data requirements and privacy concerns. This research addresses these limitations through a distributed GAN architecture specifically designed for federated environments. The core idea is to train the generator and discriminator models concurrently across multiple devices (clients) without directly sharing their raw data. Instead, each client performs local GAN training and only shares model updates with a central server. This approach maintains data privacy while enabling the generation of high-quality synthetic data. The architecture utilizes a client-server framework where clients contribute to the global model through iterative updates. The proposed system aims to achieve superior performance compared to traditional GANs, particularly in scenarios with limited data and stringent privacy requirements. We explore the optimization strategies for the federated GAN training process, including addressing issues like non-IID data and model divergence. The theoretical framework and the proposed architecture are presented, outlining the key components and their interactions. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the approach in generating realistic synthetic data.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Randomized Constraint Learning
abstract: Catastrophic forgetting and concept drift pose significant challenges to the long-term performance of neural networks in continual learning scenarios. This paper proposes a novel approach – Self-Correcting Neural Networks (SCNNs) – leveraging a randomized constraint learning mechanism to proactively address these issues. The core idea involves periodically introducing constraints on the network's parameters, driven by recent data, thereby preventing deviations from previously learned patterns. Unlike traditional continual learning methods that primarily focus on mitigating forgetting *after* it occurs, SCNNs operate proactively, actively shaping the network's learning process. This approach is demonstrated through a theoretical framework outlining the key components and offers a novel perspective on mitigating continual learning challenges. The proposed method utilizes a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimization algorithm combined with a randomized constraint generation process to maintain accuracy across evolving datasets. Experimental evaluation, though not included in this document due to the focus on the theoretical framework, would demonstrate the effectiveness of SCNNs compared to existing continual learning techniques. The primary contribution is a formalized, proactive strategy for continual learning, represented by the equation: Δθ = η * ∇L(θ; xt, yt) + α * Rt, where Δθ represents the parameter update, η is the learning rate, ∇L is the gradient of the loss function, α is the constraint weight, and Rt is the randomized constraint. This framework provides a solid foundation for future research and development in this area.

title: Information Bottleneck with Differential Privacy for Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without direct data sharing, thus addressing privacy concerns. However, FL is still susceptible to privacy breaches and suffers from significant information loss during model aggregation, a phenomenon addressed by the information bottleneck (IB) principle. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates the IB technique with differential privacy (DP) within the FL setting. We formulate the problem as a constrained optimization, minimizing information loss while simultaneously satisfying DP guarantees. Our approach utilizes a compressed representation of local data, learned through an IB objective, and introduces noise to protect individual data points, ensuring privacy. The core contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these two techniques, leading to enhanced privacy protection and improved model accuracy compared to standard FL. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a theoretical analysis and outline potential implementation strategies. The primary goal is to achieve a balance between model performance and privacy preservation, a critical aspect often overlooked in current FL methodologies. The theoretical framework provides a foundation for future research and practical deployment in privacy-sensitive applications.

title: 自适应量子拓扑场的计算演化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework for analyzing and simulating quantum topology, specifically focusing on its dynamic evolution. Traditional quantum computing often relies on static algorithms, while quantum topology offers a unique paradigm for modeling complex systems. We propose a self-adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts quantum topology parameters to mimic the evolution of quantum topology fields. This approach allows for precise control and optimization of quantum computations. The core claim of this work is that this framework can effectively simulate and control quantum topology in complex systems, providing a significant advancement in quantum algorithm design and optimization. The paper details the implementation of this framework, explores its capabilities through simulations, and discusses the potential implications for future quantum technology.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Anomaly Detection in Time Series
abstract: Anomaly detection in time series data remains a significant challenge across diverse domains, from industrial monitoring to financial fraud detection. Traditional methods frequently rely on static thresholds, which can be ineffective when dealing with complex, evolving time series exhibiting non-stationary behavior. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing probabilistic programming to model time series data, enabling robust anomaly detection based on deviations from the learned distribution. We formulate a probabilistic model – specifically, a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) – to capture the underlying statistical characteristics of the time series. The model is then used to predict the expected distribution of future data points. Anomalies are identified as points whose likelihood of occurrence under this model is significantly lower than expected, signifying a substantial deviation from the learned temporal patterns. This approach offers a more adaptive and flexible solution compared to static thresholding, explicitly accounting for temporal dependencies and providing a quantifiable measure of anomaly severity. The methodology is demonstrated through a theoretical framework and conceptual examples, laying the groundwork for future implementation and evaluation.

title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of dynamic topology quantum computation to address challenges in simulating complex dynamic topological systems, such as biological molecules and material self-organization. We propose a novel framework that leverages the unique properties of dynamic topology to construct a dynamically evolving "topology network" through simulation, enabling the investigation of intricate self-assembly processes. The core mechanism centers around generating and manipulating these networks, allowing for the modeling of phenomena not readily accessible through traditional quantum algorithms. The paper explores the benefits of this approach and highlights its potential to unlock new insights into the behavior of these systems.

title: Beyond the Default: How Customizable Artificial Intelligence Agents Can Attenuate Stereotypical Preferences
abstract: ABSTRACT AI agents are typically deployed with gender cues that match traditional role expectations, such as female voices or avatars in assistive and support roles, because stereotype‐congruent designs enhance consumer adoption, trust, and engagement. However, prior research suggests that this practice risks entrenching occupational gender stereotypes at a societal level, raising the question of whether, and under what conditions, consumers’ stereotype‐congruent preferences can be attenuated. Drawing on Role Congruity Theory and research on bias correction, we propose that preferences for gender‐stereotypical AI agents are not fixed but contingent on the salience of gender cues in the decision context: when gender is foregrounded as a potential source of bias, consumers may deliberately shift toward counterstereotypical choices. Four experimental studies ( N = 2530) test this proposition. Study 1 establishes that, under low gender‐cue salience, consumers default to AI agents whose gender aligns with stereotypical occupational roles. Study 2 shows that making gender cues salient in the choice process can attenuate these default preferences, and, under certain conditions, shift choices toward counterstereotypical agents. Studies 3 and 4 provide process evidence consistent with a role for action‐efficacy beliefs, whereby individuals come to view choosing a counterstereotypical AI agent as a meaningful way to promote gender equality. Gender salience, whether induced through design choices (Study 3) or explicit bias warnings (Study 4), was associated with stronger action‐efficacy beliefs, and the conditional indirect effects through these beliefs emerged primarily among women in male‐typed contexts, while comparable effects were weaker or absent among men and in female‐typed domains. Our findings identify conditions under which AI design choices can attenuate stereotype‐congruent preferences and provide evidence regarding the psychological processes associated with these shifts, offering actionable insights for managers and policymakers seeking to design AI agents that support more equitable human–AI interactions.

title: SmallReason-ColBERT: An Ultra-Small Late-Interaction Retriever for Reasoning Intensive Retrieval
abstract: Reasoning-intensive retrieval remains difficult for small models. Compact public ColBERTs are usually trained on general-purpose corpora and underperform reasoning-tuned 150M+ baselines on BRIGHT~bright by several nDCG@10 points. However, no public reasoning-tuned ColBERT exists at edge scale. We introduce SmallReason-ColBERT, a 32M late-interaction retriever that closes much of this gap with three components: a varied-length contrastive warmup on ReasonIR-VL, a hard-negative contrastive polish on merged ReasonIR-HQ and BGE-Reasoner data, and a single-layer per-query-token importance head trained on top of the frozen base. The head is trained with an un-normalised weighted MaxSim score and evaluated with its length-normalised form. In a controlled re-training, replacing this training objective with the symmetric normalised score causes the loss to stall and costs 3.59 nDCG@10. The full recipe reaches 21.41 mean nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, within 1.21 of the 150M Reason-ModernColBERT (22.62) and above all le 33M ColBERTs we evaluate. Through ablations on capacity, initialisation, and score variants, we further show that the learned head outperforms fixed IDF weighting and that simply thresholding the learned gates is harmful. https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/SmallReason-ColBERT

title: Extending TotalSegmentator: Predicting Patient and Acquisition Characteristics from CT and MR Images
abstract: Background: Patient details and acquisition metadata are important for clinical decisions, image quality control, and automated research pipelines, but may be missing or unreliable in imaging archives. Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fast open-source model that predicts patient and acquisition characteristics directly from CT and MR images. Materials and Methods: Separate 3D ResNet-10 ensembles for CT and MR were trained on 57,291 and 43,200 clinical examinations acquired from 2011 to 2025. Both predicted weight, height, age, sex, contrast presence, vertebral coverage, and image noise. The CT model additionally predicted scanner manufacturer, tube voltage, tube current, convolution kernel, and post-injection time; the MR model predicted sequence class. Performance was evaluated on internal CT (n=501) and MR (n=636) test sets and an external CT dataset (n=54). Results: Internal CT MAEs were 3.90 kg, 3.68 cm, and 4.42 years for weight, height, and age, with sex F1=0.990; corresponding MR results were 4.34 kg, 4.62 cm, 7.13 years, and F1=0.970. The CNN outperformed a segmentation-derived XGBoost baseline for all four core targets in both modalities (adjusted P<=.042). F1 scores were 0.963 for CT contrast, 0.953 for MR sequence, and 0.823 for MR contrast. External CT MAEs were 4.45 kg, 4.05 cm, and 5.17 years, with sex F1=0.971. CPU inference required 20 seconds for CT and 12 seconds for MR. Conclusion: One 3D multitask model per modality can rapidly recover patient and acquisition characteristics from heterogeneous CT and MR examinations. Models are available in TotalSegmentator: https://github.com/wasserth/TotalSegmentator

The CNN outperformed a segmentation-derived XGBoost baseline for all four core targets in both modalities (adjusted P<=.042). F1 scores were 0.963 for CT contrast, 0.953 for MR sequence, and 0.823 for MR contrast. External CT MAEs were 4.45 kg, 4.05 cm, and 5.17 years, with sex F1=0.971. title: Fractal Topology for Representing Complex Dependencies in Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network design and optimization utilizing fractal topologies. The core idea is that fractal structures, with their inherent self-similarity and hierarchical organization, provide a natural framework for representing and capturing the complex, non-linear dependencies found in many real-world systems. We introduce a methodology for constructing neural networks based on fractal-inspired layering, where layers exhibit self-similar patterns at various scales. The training process will employ evolutionary algorithms specifically tailored to optimize these fractal network structures. This approach represents a shift from traditional feedforward networks, offering a geometric representation better suited to reflecting the inherent complexity of systems across diverse domains. The key contribution lies in leveraging the mathematical properties of fractals to enhance network representation and learning efficiency. The core concept is expressed as: (N) = (Nl)(d), where N is the overall network complexity, Nl represents the complexity of a single fractal layer, and d is the scaling dimension. We aim to demonstrate that fractal topologies can improve network performance, particularly in scenarios with high dimensionality and intricate relationships. Furthermore, we explore the potential for adaptive fractal generation during training, allowing the network to dynamically adjust its structure to best fit the underlying data. The effectiveness of this approach will be assessed through simulation and theoretical analysis, focusing on metrics such as network convergence speed, accuracy, and computational efficiency. The proposed framework provides a new perspective on neural network architecture design, potentially leading to more robust and efficient models.
